1.pericope_label: Forasmuch then as Christ hath suffered for us in the flesh, arm yourselves likewise with the same mind: for he that hath suffered in the flesh hath ceased from sin; that he no longer should live the rest of his time in the flesh to the lusts of men, but to the will of God.

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin take the sufferings and the rule of living. Gill says the apostle, having finished his digression concerning Christ's preaching in the ministry of Noah and concerning baptism, returns to the sufferings of Christ he had before mentioned and argues from them to holiness of life and patience in sufferings: seeing that Christ, the eternal Son of God, the Lord of glory, the holy and Just One, suffered such indignities, reproaches and persecutions from men, the wrath of God, the curses of the law and death itself, and that not for himself nor for angels but for men, and those not all men, otherwise his death with respect to some must be in vain, but for a particular number of men described in the beginning of this epistle as elect according to the foreknowledge of God. These sufferings he endured in the room and stead of those persons, in the days of his flesh, while here on earth, and in his human nature. On the next verse Gill notes that the Arabic version reads, that ye no longer should live, and says the clause expresses the end of being armed with the thought that a suffering saint after death is clear of sin, and the use to be made of it in the remainder of life, that such a person, guarded against the fears of death, should no longer live as before. Calvin says that when the apostle had before set Christ before us he spoke only of the suffering of the cross, since the cross sometimes means mortification, because the outward man is wasted by afflictions and our flesh is subdued; but he now ascends higher, for he speaks of the reformation of the whole man. Scripture recommends to us a twofold likeness to the death of Christ, that we are to be conformed to him in reproaches and troubles, and also that, the old man being dead and extinct in us, we are to be renewed to a spiritual life; yet Christ is not simply to be viewed as our example when we speak of the mortification of the flesh, for it is by his Spirit that we are really made conformable to his death, so that it becomes effectual to the crucifying of our flesh. We are really and effectually supplied with invincible weapons to subdue the flesh, Calvin says, if we partake as we ought of the efficacy of Christ's death. The particle does not, he thinks, denote here the cause but is to be taken as explanatory, for Peter sets forth what that thought or mind is with which Christ's death arms us, even that the dominion of sin ought to be abolished in us so that God may reign in our life. Erasmus has incorrectly, as Calvin thinks, rendered the word he who did suffer, applying it to Christ; for it is an indefinite sentence, which generally extends to all the godly and has the same meaning as the words of Paul that he who is dead is justified or freed from sin, both Apostles intimating that when we become dead to the flesh we have no more to do with sin, that it should reign in us. On the next verse Calvin says the apostle sets forth the way of ceasing from sin, that renouncing the covetings of men we should study to form our life according to the will of God, and thus includes the two things in which renovation consists, the destruction of the flesh and the vivification of the spirit; the course of good living is to begin with the former, but we are to advance to the latter. Peter here defines the rule of right living, even that man depends on the will of God, from which it follows that nothing is right and well ordered in man's life as soon as he wanders from this rule; and we ought to notice the contrast between the lusts of men and the will of God, from which we understand how great is our depravity.

Henry says the apostle draws a new inference from the consideration of Christ's sufferings: as he had before made use of it to persuade to patience in suffering, so here to mortification of sin. The word flesh in the former part of the verse signifies Christ's human nature, but in the latter part it signifies man's corrupt nature, so that the sense is, as Christ suffered in his human nature, do you, according to your baptismal vow and profession, make your corrupt nature suffer, by putting to death the body of sin by self-denial and mortification. Henry draws two lessons. Some of the strongest and best arguments against all sorts of sin are taken from the sufferings of Christ, since all sympathy and tenderness for Christ as a sufferer are lost if you do not put away sin: he died to destroy it, and though he could cheerfully submit to the worst sufferings, yet he could never submit to the least sin. And the beginning of all true mortification lies in the mind, not in penances and hardships upon the body, for the mind of man is carnal and full of enmity, and the understanding is darkened, being alienated from the life of God, till he be renewed by the regenerating grace of God. On the next verse Henry says the apostle explains being dead to sin both negatively and positively: negatively, a Christian ought no longer to live the rest of his time in the flesh to the sinful lusts and corrupt desires of carnal wicked men; positively, he ought to conform himself to the revealed will of the holy God. The lusts of men, he adds, are the springs of all their wickedness, since whatever occasional temptations may be, they could not prevail were it not for men's own corruptions; and all good Christians make the will of God, not their own lusts or desires, the rule of their lives and actions.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson take the arming, the text and the grammar. Barnes says the design was to set the suffering Redeemer before them as an example in their trials, and that the chapter as a whole relates to the manner in which those to whom the apostle wrote ought to bear their trials and to the encouragements to a holy life notwithstanding their persecutions. His great solicitude was that if they suffered it should not be for crime, and that their enemies should not be able to bring any well-founded accusation against them. On the next verse Barnes says the believer has become, through the death of Christ, dead to the world and to the former things which influenced him, in order that he should hereafter live not to the lusts of the flesh; the rest of his time in the flesh is the remainder of the time he is to live on the earth, and the lusts of men are such as men commonly live for and indulge in. The object of redemption, he adds, is to rescue us from being swayed by wicked lusts and to bring us to be conformed wholly to the will of God. Ellicott renders the opening as a participial phrase, Christ then having suffered in or to the flesh, that is so far as the flesh is concerned, the word then taking us back to the words killed in the flesh of the previous chapter. It is difficult, he says, to decide about the right of the words for us to stand in the text: Tischendorf and Lachmann strike them out and are probably right in doing so, and the authority for the reading for you is nearly as strong, but in fact neither is wanted here, as the point is not the atoning character of Christ's death but the death itself. The word rendered mind he would render conception: it does not mean merely put yourselves into the same disposition, that is, resolve to die with Him, for though the word may possibly bear the meaning intent assigned to it at Hebrews 4:12, the only other place in the New Testament where it occurs, the more natural and common sense is that of conception, notion, view. Christ is therefore said to have been armed with a particular conception or view, which He found to be a sufficient shield in the day of suffering, and we are exhorted to try the same defensive armour; the view which Christ found so efficacious was the view He took of the suffering itself. The clause about ceasing Ellicott would render, that he that hath suffered to the flesh is at rest from sin, the thought being probably derived from Romans 6:7: the death of the body puts a stop, at any rate for the redeemed, to any further possibility of sin. A slight difficulty is caused by the implied fact that Christ too in dying ceased from sin; but the Greek word literally means hath been caused to rest, Peter using expressly, for the only time in the New Testament, that part of the verb which does not mean a voluntary cessation from what one was doing before, but a pause imposed from without. That Christ looked upon His death as a boon of rest from sin, Ellicott says, though it does not say from sinning, is not only a true and impressive thought but is fully justified by Romans 6:10, where he died unto sin, and even by His cry that it is finished. On the next verse Ellicott says the Greek admits at least equally of the translation, that ye no longer, so that the second verse attaches itself not to the clause about him that hath suffered but to the clause arm yourselves; and unless this be understood we become involved in the difficulty that whereas up to this point the apostle has been urging the future martyrs by the example of Christ to face the death of the body bravely, he would now be sliding confusedly into treating of the baptismal death to sin, and indeed actually saying that a martyr's death was a step to leading the rest of the life on earth becomingly. Attached to the arming, it runs without confusion: as Christ suffered to the flesh without shrinking, take for your protection and support the same thought which proved a protection and support to Him, that to be rid of sin for ever was the greatest of all possible blessings and is only attainable through the bodily death, and the result of embracing this thought will be that for the rest of your lives on earth you may no longer live to men's lusts but to God's will. Robertson notes the genitive absolute with the second aorist participle of the verb to suffer and the locative of the word for flesh, and says the particle then draws and applies the main lesson of the preceding chapter, the fact that Christ suffered for us. The verb rendered arm ye yourselves is a direct middle first aorist imperative of an old verb from the word for weapon, used here in a metaphorical sense and found only here in the New Testament, and the noun rendered mind is an old word for putting in mind, thinking, will, occurring in the New Testament only here and at Hebrews 4:12. The perfect middle of the verb to make cease is followed by the ablative singular for sin, though one manuscript reads the dative plural; temptation, Robertson adds, has lost its appeal and power with such a man. On the next verse he takes the clause as a purpose clause with the first aorist active infinitive of an old verb meaning to spend a life, found only here in the New Testament, and the accusative of time with an old adjective meaning remaining in addition, also only here; the construction can also express result.

Clarke and Wesley take the pattern and survey the readings. Clarke says Christ is our proper pattern and we should have the same disposition he had, the same forgiving spirit, with meekness, gentleness and complete self-possession. On the words about ceasing from sin he offers four accounts. Understood literally, this is a general maxim: the man who suffers generally reflects on his ways, is humbled, fears approaching death, loathes himself because of his past iniquities and ceases from them, for in a state of suffering the mind loses its relish for the sins of the flesh, because they are embittered to him through the apprehension which he has of death and judgment. Some suppose the words mean that those who have firmly resolved, if called to it, to suffer death rather than apostatize from Christianity have consequently ceased from, or are delivered from, the sin of saving their lives at the expense of their faith. Others think it a passage parallel to Romans 6:7 and interpret it, he that hath mortified the flesh hath ceased from sin. Dr Bentley, Clarke reports, applies the whole to our redemption by Christ, that he that hath suffered in the flesh hath died for our sins; but this, Clarke says, seems a very constrained sense. On the next verse he takes living to the lusts of men as being governed by the base principle of giving up one's faith to save one's life, according to the will of the idolatrous persecutors, whereas the will of God is that a man should retain the truth and live according to its dictates though he should suffer for it. Wesley says the same mind will be armour of proof against all your enemies, and that he that hath suffered in the flesh is he that hath so suffered as to be thereby made inwardly and truly conformable to the sufferings of Christ, and so is delivered from sin.

debates: Whether the words for us belong to the text. Ellicott alone raises the question, reports that Tischendorf and Lachmann strike them out and thinks them probably right, notes that the authority for reading for you is nearly as strong, and holds that neither is wanted since the point is the death itself and not its atoning character; Gill, on the contrary, builds particular redemption on the phrase, arguing that Christ suffered not for all men, else his death with respect to some must be in vain, but for the elect.

What having ceased from sin means. Clarke sets out four accounts, the general maxim that suffering weans a man from sin, the resolve of the martyr who has ceased from the sin of saving his life at the cost of his faith, the parallel with Romans 6:7 about mortifying the flesh, and the reading that refers the whole to Christ's own death, which he ascribes to Bentley and calls very constrained; Calvin rejects that last reading independently, ascribing it to Erasmus and answering that the sentence is indefinite and extends to all the godly; Robertson says temptation has lost its appeal with such a man.

Whether the second verse reads he or ye. Ellicott says the Greek admits the plural at least equally and argues for it, since otherwise the apostle slides from urging martyrs to face bodily death into the baptismal death to sin and is left making a martyr's death a step towards living the rest of one's life becomingly; Robertson renders the plural; Gill reports that the Arabic version reads it so; Barnes and Henry keep the singular.
outliers: Ellicott alone answers a theological difficulty from grammar, meeting the implication that Christ too ceased from sin by observing that the apostle uses the part of the verb which means not a voluntary stopping but a rest imposed from without, so that death was to Christ a boon of rest from sin though not from sinning.
Henry alone locates the whole force of the verse in a shift of sense within one word, the flesh meaning Christ's human nature in the first half and man's corrupt nature in the second.

3.pericope_label: For the time past of our life may suffice us to have wrought the will of the Gentiles, when we walked in lasciviousness, lusts, excess of wine, revellings, banquetings, and abominable idolatries.

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin question the pronoun and defend the catalogue. Gill says the word our is left out in the Alexandrian copy and in the Vulgate Latin and Syriac versions, while the Arabic version reads, the time of your past life, and the Ethiopic to the same purpose; and this seems to him the more agreeable reading, since it can hardly be thought that the apostle would put himself among the Jews dispersed among the Gentiles who had walked with them in their unregeneracy in all the sins hereafter mentioned, and it best agrees with the following verse. Calvin says Peter does not mean that we ought to be wearied with pleasures, as those are wont to be who are filled with them to satiety, but that on the contrary the memory of our past life ought to stimulate us to repentance; and doubtless it ought to be the sharpest goad to make us run on well, when we recollect that we have been wandering from the right way the greatest part of our life. Peter reminds us that it would be most unreasonable were we not to change the course of our life after having been enlightened by Christ, making a distinction between the time of ignorance and the time of faith, as though he had said that it was but right they should become new and different men from the time that Christ had called them. Instead of the covetings of men he now mentions the will of the Gentiles, by which he reproves the Jews for having mixed with the Gentiles in all their pollutions, though the Lord had separated them from the Gentiles. In what follows he shows that those vices ought to be put off which prove men to be blind and ignorant of God, and there is a peculiar emphasis in the words, for he intimates that we ought to persevere to the end, since we have been redeemed by the Lord for this end, that we may serve him all the days of our life. He does not give the whole catalogue of sins but mentions only some, and names the grosser vices, as is usually done when examples are adduced. But here a question arises, Calvin says, since Peter seems to have done wrong to many in making all men guilty of lasciviousness, dissipation, lusts, drunkenness and revellings, for it is certain that all were not involved in these vices, and we know that some among the Gentiles lived honourably and without a spot of infamy. To this he replies that Peter does not so ascribe these vices to the Gentiles as though he charged every individual with all of them, but that we are by nature inclined to all these evils, and not only so, but that we are so much under the power of depravity that these fruits which he mentions necessarily proceed from it as from an evil root. There is indeed no one, Calvin adds, who has not within him the seed of all vices, but all do not germinate and grow up in every individual, though the contagion is so spread and diffused through the whole human race that the whole community appears infected.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson handle the text, the terms and the readership. Barnes paraphrases the opening as, we have spent sufficient time in indulging ourselves and following our wicked propensities, and we should hereafter live in a different manner; this does not mean that it was ever proper thus to live, but that we have had enough of these things, and he matches it with a line of Horace to the same effect. To have wrought the will of the Gentiles does not mean to be subservient to their will, but to have done what they willed to do, that is, to live as they did. The apostle says we, Barnes notes, not as meaning that he himself had been addicted to these vices but as speaking of those who were Christians in general, since it is common to say that we lived so and so when speaking of a collection of persons without meaning that each one was guilty of all the practices enumerated; the use of we would show that the apostle did not mean to set himself up as better than they were, but was willing to be identified with them. On the word rendered excess of wine, which occurs nowhere else in the New Testament, Barnes says it properly means an overflowing of wine, and hence wine-drinking or drunkenness, and that this was a common vice need not be proved, since multitudes of those who became Christians had been drunkards and intemperance abounded in all the heathen world. It should not be inferred from the English translation, he cautions, that wine is improper only when used to excess, or that the moderate use of wine is proper: whatever may be true on that point, nothing can be determined in regard to it from the use of this word, since the apostle had his eye on one thing only, such a use of wine as led to intoxication, about the impropriety of which there could be no doubt. Ellicott says there are two words in the English which do not stand in the true text and sadly impede the sense, of our life and us: the first is added by some scribe to point the contrast with the rest of his time, and the second, which should be you if anything at all, is simply put to fill the gap after the word suffice; if they were right we should have Peter, quite unlike his wont, identifying himself with the bad life here described as though he himself had shared in it. The word rendered may suffice is the same as in Matthew and would be, literally, for sufficient is the past, and there is an irony in it similar to that in the third chapter. The verb rendered to have wrought he would render to have perpetrated, since the Greek word denotes the accomplishment of a criminal purpose. Just as in the previous verse there was a contrast between man's manifold and conflicting lusts and God's unity of will, so there is a contrast now between God's will and the heathen's wish, for the Greek word is quite different: to have perpetrated the heathen's wish means to have done the bad things which the heathen wanted them to be guilty of, the heathen being fain to catch them at malpractices. The words when we walked are a participle in Greek which gives no support to the use of we, but means simply having proceeded, and does not directly state that they had so proceeded, since the participle explains the foregoing verb. Lasciviousness should be plural, expressing the repeated acts of sin, and the word in Greek means any outrageous debauchery, so that it may be said to include all the words that follow; excess of wine should in like manner be plural, and is a contemptuous word, wine-swillings, differing from the word translated banquetings because the latter is more refined and also implies company, while revellings might mean any roystering parties but contains more of the notion of making a pretext of a meal. Abominable idolatries, Ellicott says, are so called not as idolatries but because of the abominable adjuncts of the idol-festivals; and this clause is the main support of those who think that the Letter was written to converts from heathenism and not from Judaism, since it is urged that Peter could not have said to persons brought up as Jews that the time past was long enough for them to have proceeded in abominable idolatries. Robertson parses the perfect active participle of the verb to go by and calls the verbal adjective rendered may suffice late and rare, occurring in the New Testament only here and twice in Matthew and apparently referring to Christ's words there, possibly an axiom or proverb. The correct text, he says, has the word for the thing desired rather than the word for will; Jews sometimes fell in with the ways of Gentiles, as today some Christians copy the ways of the world. The word for winebibbings is an old compound from the words for wine and to bubble up, meaning drunkenness, and occurring here only in the New Testament; revellings is an old word for rioting drinking parties, and carousings an old word for a drinking carousal, here only in the New Testament. In the light of these words, Robertson adds, it seems strange to find modern Christians justifying their personal liberty to drink and carouse, to say nothing of the prohibition law; the Greeks actually carried lust and drunkenness into their religious observances. To the Christian all idolatry is abominable and not allowed, but particularly those forms associated with drinking and licentiousness; the only other New Testament example of the word is by Peter also, in Acts, and about the Mosaic law, which may be the idea here, for Jews often fell into idolatrous practices.

Clarke and Wesley take the catalogue as it stands. Clarke calls the verse a complete epitome of the Gentile or heathen state and a proof that those had been Gentiles to whom the apostle wrote, and numbers six items with their Greek. They walked in lasciviousness, every species of lechery, lewdness and impurity; in lusts, strong irregular appetites and desires of all kinds; in excess of wine, a word compounded of wine and a verb meaning to be hot or to boil, so that they were inflamed with wine and in continual debauches; in revellings, lascivious feastings with drunken songs; in banquetings, wine feasts and drinking matches; and in abominable idolatries, that is, the abominations practised at their idol feasts, where they not only worshipped the idol but did it with the most impure and obscene rites. This, Clarke says, was the general state of the Gentile world, and with this monstrous wickedness Christianity had everywhere to struggle. Wesley asks whether the words revellings and banquetings have any meaning now, and answers that they had seventeen hundred years ago: then the former meant meetings to eat, meetings the direct end of which was to please the taste, and the latter meetings to drink, both of which Christians then ranked with abominable idolatries.

debates: Whether the words our and us belong to the text. Gill reports our absent from the Alexandrian copy and from the Latin and Syriac versions, and prefers the Arabic reading, the time of your past life; Ellicott strikes out both of our life and us, holding the first a scribe's addition and the second a filler, and argues that otherwise the apostle identifies himself with a life he never led; Barnes defends the received text and explains the pronoun as the common way of speaking of a body of people without charging each with all.

What to have wrought the will of the Gentiles means. Barnes says it is not subservience to their will but doing what they did; Ellicott makes the word a wish rather than a will, so that the clause means doing the bad things the heathen wanted them to be guilty of, the heathen being fain to catch them at malpractices; Robertson notes only that the correct text has the word for the thing desired.

Who the readers were. Clarke takes the catalogue for proof that they had been Gentiles; Ellicott reports the same argument as the main support of those who hold the letter written to converts from heathenism; Gill and Calvin keep the Jewish readership and explain the sins by mixture with the Gentiles, Calvin saying the apostle reproves the Jews for mingling in their pollutions; Robertson says Jews often fell into idolatrous practices.

How far the verse bears on the use of wine. Barnes cautions that nothing can be determined from the word about the moderate use of wine, the apostle having his eye only on such use as led to intoxication; Robertson finds it strange that modern Christians justify a personal liberty to drink and carouse; Wesley ranks meetings to eat and meetings to drink with abominable idolatries; Ellicott confines himself to the philology, calling the term a contemptuous one.
outliers: Calvin alone anticipates the objection that the catalogue slanders honourable heathen, and answers it not by narrowing the charge but by widening it, holding that every man carries the seed of all these vices though not all germinate in every individual.

Ellicott alone reverses the direction of the phrase, making the Gentiles' will not the pattern the readers copied but the outcome the heathen hoped for, since they were fain to catch the Christians at malpractices.

4.pericope_label: Wherein they think it strange that ye run not with them to the same excess of riot, speaking evil of you: who shall give account to him that is ready to judge the quick and the dead.

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin fortify the readers against the world's judgment. Gill says the apostle here points out what the saints must expect from the men of the world by living a different life, and mentions it to prevent discouragements, that they might not be uneasy and distressed when they observed it: the world would wonder at the change in their conversations, look on it as something new and unheard of, and treat them as strangers, yea, as enemies, on that account. On the next verse Gill says the slanderers shall give account of all their blasphemies and hard speeches spoken against God, Christ, the Gospel and good men, and receive their just punishment; and the apostle says this to calm the minds of God's people and make them sit easy under all censures, reproaches and calumnies, and not think of avenging themselves, but commit themselves to him that will judge righteously. Calvin says the word means to stop at a thing as new and unusual, a way of speaking which the Latins also sometimes use, as when Cicero says that he was a stranger in the city because he knew not what was carried on there. In this place, Calvin says, Peter fortifies the faithful lest they should suffer themselves to be disturbed or corrupted by the perverse judgments or words of the ungodly; for it is no light temptation when they among whom we live charge us that our life is different from that of mankind in general, saying that these must form for themselves a new world, for they differ from all mankind, and thus accusing the children of God as though they attempted a separation from the whole world. The Apostle anticipated this and forbade the faithful to be discouraged by such reproaches and calumnies, proposing to them as a support the judgment of God; for this it is that can sustain us against all assaults, when we patiently wait for that day in which Christ will punish all those who now presumptuously condemn us, and will show that we and our cause are approved by him. He expressly mentions the dead, Calvin adds, lest we should think that we shall suffer any loss if they remain alive when we are dead, for they shall not for this reason escape the hand of God.

Henry sets out the visible change and the world's response to it. Those who were represented in the foregoing verse as having been very wicked no longer run on in the same courses or with the same companions as they used to do, and hereupon their wicked acquaintance behave in two ways. They think it strange, being surprised and wondering at it as at something new and unusual, that their old friends should be so much altered and not run with as much violence as they used to do to the same excess of riot. And they speak evil of them, their surprise carrying them to blasphemy: they speak evil of their persons, of their way, their religion and their God. Henry draws three lessons. Those that are once really converted will not return to their former course of life, though ever so much tempted by the frowns or flatteries of others. The temper and behaviour of true Christians seem very strange to ungodly men, since that they should despise that which every one else is fond of, that they should believe many things which to others seem incredible, that they should delight in what is irksome and tedious, be zealous where they have no visible interest to serve, and depend so much upon hope, is what the ungodly cannot comprehend. And the best actions of religious people cannot escape the censures and slanders of those who are irreligious, for those actions which cost a good man the most pains, hazard and self-denial shall be most censured by the uncharitable world. For the comfort of the servants of God, Henry adds, it is here said that all wicked people, especially those who speak evil of such as are not as bad as themselves, shall give an account to him who is ready to judge, who is both able and duly authorized, and who will ere long judge and pass sentence upon all who shall then be found alive and all such as being dead shall then be raised again.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson explain the surprise and the judgment. Barnes says that in respect to these vices they who were once partners now think it strange that the readers no longer unite with them, and do not understand why they have left them, regarding them as abandoning a course of life which has much to attract for a severe and gloomy superstition. This is a true account of the feelings which the people of the world have when their companions leave them and become Christians; even the kindred of the Saviour regarded him as beside himself, and Festus supposed that Paul was mad, and the epithets of fool, enthusiast and fanatic frequently occur to the heart even if they are not always allowed to escape from the lips. The reasons they esteem it strange, Barnes says, are three. They do not appreciate the motives which influence those who leave them, feeling that it is proper to enjoy the world and not understanding what it is to act under a deep sense of responsibility to God and with reference to eternity; they live for themselves and have never been accustomed to direct the mind onward to another world and to the account they must render. They do not yet see the guilt and folly of sinful pleasures, not being convinced of the deep sinfulness of the human soul. And they do not see the force of the argument for religion. On the next verse Barnes says they shall not do this with impunity, being guilty of a great wrong for which they must answer to God. The phrase rendered ready to judge is used elsewhere of Paul saying he was ready not to be bound only but to die at Jerusalem; the meaning is not that God was about to judge, or that the day of judgment was near at hand, whatever the apostle may have supposed to be true on that point, but that he was prepared for it, all the arrangements being made with reference to it and there being nothing to hinder it. The quick and the dead are the living and the dead, that is, those who shall be alive when he comes and those in their graves, a common phrase to denote all who shall be brought before the bar of God; and the meaning in this connexion seems to be that they should bear their trials patiently, not attempting to avenge themselves, since the Lord would vindicate them when he came to judgment. Ellicott says the word wherein is used exactly as in the second chapter: it does not directly point back to the list of sins just named, but the grammatical antecedent is to be supplied in the participial clause which follows, so that the sense is, in a particular where they cannot imagine your not being as bad as themselves, slanderously affirming that you are. The only difficulty involved is one which does not show in the English, that the participle is attracted into the nominative case by the influence of the finite verb instead of standing in the genitive agreeing with of the Gentiles; but Peter deals very freely with participles in the nominative case, as at several places earlier in the letter, and like instances are not wanting in classical Greek. On the next verse Ellicott says the words about giving account are perhaps said with a reference to the third chapter, where these very persons call the Christians to give account, the Greek word being the same; and the side-purpose of the clause is to warn the readers against sharing their fate by sharing their sins. The clause about him that is ready to judge carries on the history of Jesus Christ a step further still, since the last thing was his sitting on the right hand of God, and this is the order of the Apostles' Creed. Ellicott quotes the wise remark of Bengel that the Apostles, when they are not expressly treating of the date of Christ's advent, set forth that advent to their longing and devotion as close at hand, so that Peter includes the slanderers of his day among the living, as just about to be judged. Robertson takes the opening phrase as in which thing, that is, manner of life, and parses the present passive of an old verb from the word for stranger, meaning to entertain a guest and so to astonish: they are surprised or astonished. The clause that ye run not with them is a genitive absolute with the present active participle of an old compound meaning to run together like a crowd or a mob, just like our phrase about running with certain folks. The noun rendered excess is a late and rare word meaning our overflowing, here only in the New Testament, and the noun rendered riot is the character of an abandoned man, an old word for a dissolute life. Robertson quotes the judgment that the Christians were compelled to stand aloof from all the social pleasures of the world, and that the Gentiles bitterly resented their puritanism, regarding them as the enemies of all joy and therefore of the human race. On the next verse he notes the future active of the verb to give back with the word for account, and says the correct text is, to the one readily judging, rather than to the one ready to judge, which softens the rugged original; that is Christ apparently, though the Father in the first chapter. The quick and the dead are the living and the dead, those living at the time and those already dead.

Clarke and Wesley gloss the words and divide the quick from the dead. Clarke says the word rendered think it strange means that they wonder and are astonished at the readers, that they can renounce these gratifications of the flesh for a spiritual something the good of which they cannot see; the phrase rendered excess of riot is a flood of profligacy, bearing down all rule, order and restraints before it; and speaking evil of you is literally blaspheming, that is, speaking impiously against God and calumniously of the readers. On the next verse Clarke says they shall give account of these irregularities to him who is prepared to judge both the Jews and the Gentiles: the Gentiles, previously to the preaching of the Gospel among them, were reckoned to be dead in trespasses and sins, under the sentence of death because they had sinned, while the Jews had at least by their religious profession a name to live, and by that profession were bound to give account to God. Wesley glosses the excess as the same as ye did once, and supplies the terms of the slander, that they are spoken of as proud, singular, silly, wicked and the like. On the next verse he says they shall give account of this as well as of all their other ways, and that when the apostle calls him ready, so faith represents him now.

debates: What makes the change seem strange. Barnes gives three reasons, that the world cannot appreciate the motives of those who leave it, does not see the guilt and folly of sinful pleasures, and does not see the force of the argument for religion; Henry lists what puzzles them, the despising of what all are fond of, the believing of what seems incredible, the delight in what is irksome, and the dependence on hope; Robertson quotes the judgment that the Gentiles resented the Christians as enemies of all joy; Calvin reports the taunt itself, that these must form for themselves a new world.

How ready the Judge is. Barnes denies that the words mean the day was near at hand, whatever the apostle may have supposed, and takes them of preparedness only, all the arrangements being made; Ellicott sets the clause in the order of the Creed and quotes Bengel that the Apostles set the advent before their longing as close at hand, so that Peter reckons the slanderers of his own day among the living about to be judged; Robertson prefers the text, to the one readily judging, saying the smoother rendering softens the rugged original.

Who the quick and the dead are. Barnes and Robertson take them as those alive at the coming and those already dead; Calvin adds that the dead are named so that we may not think we lose anything if our slanderers outlive us; Clarke alone reads the pair of the two nations, the Gentiles dead in trespasses and sins before the Gospel came and the Jews having by profession a name to live.

What the opening word refers to. Ellicott holds that it does not point back to the list of sins but forward to the participle, giving the sense that in a particular where they cannot imagine the readers being no worse than themselves they slanderously affirm that they are, and grants that the participle stands in the wrong case; Robertson takes it simply as in which manner of life.
outliers: Robertson alone prefers the rougher of two readings on the ground of its roughness, holding that the smoother rendering of the phrase about judging softens the rugged original.
Clarke alone gives the quick and the dead a national sense rather than a temporal one, making the dead the Gentiles who were dead in trespasses and sins before the Gospel reached them.

6.pericope_label: For for this cause was the gospel preached also to them that are dead, that they might be judged according to men in the flesh, but live according to God in the spirit.

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin take the reference and the consolation. Gill says the opening words point not to what goes before, as though the gospel were preached to wicked men that they might be left without excuse, but to what follows, and that what follows does not so much design the reason of the preaching as the event consequential upon it. By the Gospel, he says, is meant the good news of the incarnation, sufferings and death of Christ and salvation by him, including all the doctrines of grace, of pardon, righteousness and eternal life; and its being preached means the publishing of it openly, freely and boldly, with faithfulness and consistency. Calvin says we see in what sense the apostle takes the former passage in the third chapter, even that death does not hinder Christ from being always our defender; and it is a remarkable consolation to the godly that death itself brings no loss to their salvation, for though Christ may not appear a deliverer in this life, yet his redemption is not void or without effect, since his power extends to the dead. The Greek word being doubtful, it may be rendered in the masculine or in the neuter, but the meaning is almost the same, that Christ had been made known as a redeemer to the dead, or that salvation had been made known to them by the gospel. But if the grace of Christ once penetrated to the dead, Calvin argues, there is no doubt but that we shall partake of it when dead; we then set for it limits much too narrow if we confine it to the present life. This has been said, as he thinks, by way of anticipation, for it might have been objected that the gospel is of no benefit to the dead, as it does not restore them to life; Peter concedes a part of this objection, and yet in such a way that they are not deprived of the salvation obtained by Christ. In the first clause, when he says that they might be judged in the flesh according to men, it is a concession, and judged means here, as often elsewhere, condemned, the flesh being the outward man; so that the meaning is that though according to the estimation of the world the dead suffer destruction in their flesh and are deemed condemned as to the outward man, yet they cease not to live with God, and that in their spirit, because Christ quickens them by his Spirit. We ought to add, Calvin says, what Paul teaches, that the Spirit is life, and hence it will be that he will at length absorb the relics of death which still cleave to us; the sum of it is that though the condition of the dead in the flesh is worse, according to man, yet it is enough that the Spirit of Christ revives them and will eventually lead them to the perfection of life. Calvin also reports that others regard the dead here as the dead in sins, and gives their several paraphrases of what follows, that they might condemn their former life and live a better, or that they might be brought to such a state of life as their carnal neighbours will look upon as a kind of condemnation and death, or that they might be condemned indeed by men in the flesh yet live by God in the Spirit.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson survey the readings. Barnes says the opening expression refers to an end to be reached or a reason why the thing referred to is done, and that the end is stated in the rest of the verse. Many, as Doddridge and Whitby, understand this of those who are spiritually dead, that is the Gentiles, supposing the object to be that they might be brought to such a state of life as their carnal neighbours will look upon as a kind of condemnation and death. Others suppose it refers to those who had suffered martyrdom in the cause of Christianity; others, following Saurin, that it refers to the sinners of the old world, expressing a hope that some of them might be saved; and others that it means that the Saviour went down and preached to those who are dead, in accordance with one of the interpretations given of the third chapter. It seems to Barnes that the most natural and obvious interpretation is to refer it to those who were then dead, to whom the gospel had been preached when living, and who had become true Christians, an interpretation proposed by Wetstein, Rosenmuller and Bloomfield. In support of this he offers three arguments: that this is the natural and obvious meaning of the word dead, which should be understood literally unless there is good reason in the connexion for departing from the common meaning; that the apostle had just used the word in that sense in the previous verse; and that this suits the connexion and accords with the design of the apostle, who was addressing those suffering persecution, so that it was natural to refer to those who had died in the faith and to show for their encouragement that though they had been put to death they still lived to God. On the second half of the verse Barnes says that so far as men are concerned, or in respect to the treatment they received from men in the flesh, they were judged and condemned, while in respect to God and the treatment they received from him they would live in spirit: men judged them severely and put them to death for their religion, and God gave them life and saved them, so that by the one they were condemned in the flesh, so far as pain and sorrow and death could be inflicted on the body, and by the other they were made to live in the spirit. Ellicott says the version is misleading and seems indeed to be one of those rare cases where the original has been expanded by the translators for doctrinal ends, since the Greek is simply, for this end was the gospel preached to the dead also, or still more literally, to dead men also. No one with an unpreoccupied mind, he says, could doubt, taking this clause by itself, that the persons to whom this preaching was made were dead at the time of being preached to; and if this is so, then Peter is carrying us back to his teaching in the third chapter and explaining further the purpose of Christ's descent. To obtain a clear notion of the hard saying, Ellicott surveys the course of the whole passage: the apostle had said it is better to suffer in well-doing than in evil-doing, gave an instance of persons who suffered in evil-doing in the fleshly Antediluvians whom God cut short by the Flood and to whom Christ went to preach in their prison-house, and then exhorted his readers, some of whom had been allowing themselves to fall into antinomian ways, not to live any longer to the flesh nor to make true the slanders of the heathen. The first question, he says, is what the apostle means to substantiate by the words for this cause: not the fact that Christ will judge the dead as well as the quick, for that would have no practical bearing upon the readers, and not the fact that Christ was now ready for judgment, since we should then have expected something more like, the reason why the dead were preached to was that the judgment might no longer be put off. Instead, the whole point of the verse is the particular destiny in reserve for those dead, which destiny was the intention and result of Christ's preaching the gospel to them, so that it must be a further reason for warning the Christians not to live lives of evil-doing like the contemporaries of Noah or their own heathen contemporaries; and if the word for is to be attached to any particular words, it may perhaps be attached to the words they shall give account. Robertson notes the impersonal use of the first aorist passive and asks whether Peter means preached to men after they are dead, or to men once alive but dead now or when the judgment comes. There are those, he says, such as Augustine and Luther, who take dead here in the spiritual sense, dead in trespasses and sins, but who consider it impossible for Peter to use the same word in two senses so close together; yet Jesus did it in the same sentence, as in the case of the word for life at Matthew 16:25. Robertson also reports the view that all men who did not hear the gospel message in this life will hear it in the next before the final judgment. He parses the purpose clause with the first aorist passive subjunctive of the verb to judge, contrasted with the present active subjunctive of the verb to live, and notes the further contrast between the phrase according to men and the phrase according to God.

Clarke and Wesley canvass the translations and prefer the antediluvians. Clarke calls this a most difficult verse and gives the three best translations he has seen. The first makes it the effect of the preaching of the Gospel to the dead, that is the unconverted Gentiles, that some will be punished as carnal men but others, those converted to Christianity, lead a spiritual life unto God. The second makes it, for this purpose hath the Gospel been preached even to the dead, that is the Gentiles, that although they might be condemned indeed by men in the flesh, their persecutors, yet they might live eternally by God in the Spirit. The third makes it, for this cause was the Gospel preached to them that were dead, that they who live according to men in the flesh may be condemned, but that they who live according to God in the Spirit may live. There are as many different translations of this verse, Clarke says, and comments upon it, as there are translators and commentators; the third appears the most simple could the Greek text bear it, but the second, which is nearly the sense given by Wesley in his Paraphrase, is more likely to be the true one among those proposed. But if the apostle had the same fact in view which he mentions in the third chapter, then the antediluvians are the persons intended: because Christ is prepared to judge the quick and the dead and to dispense righteous judgment in consequence of having afforded them every necessary advantage, the Gospel was preached by Noah to them also who are dead, the antediluvian world, then dead in trespasses and sins and condemned to death by the righteous judgment of God; but in his great compassion he afforded them a respite, that though they were condemned as men in the flesh, yet, hearing this Gospel by Noah, they might believe and live according to God in the Spirit, a blessed life in eternity according to the mercy of God who sent his Spirit to strive with them. This appears to Clarke the most consistent sense, especially as the apostle seems to refer to what he had said of the Spirit of Christ in Noah preaching to the spirits in prison. Wesley says the gospel was preached to this end ever since it was given to Adam, and that they that are now dead were preached to in their several generations; they might be judged, that is though they were judged, in the flesh according to the manner of men, with rash, unrighteous judgment, yet they might live according to the will and word of God in the Spirit, the soul renewed after his image.

debates: Whether the dead are dead in sin or dead in body. Barnes reports Doddridge and Whitby taking them for the spiritually dead, that is the Gentiles, and Clarke gives two renderings on the same footing; Robertson traces the spiritual sense to Augustine and Luther, reports the objection that the apostle could not use one word in two senses so close together, and answers that Christ did exactly that within a single sentence; Ellicott holds that no one with an unpreoccupied mind could doubt that those preached to were dead at the time.

Which dead are meant, if the word is literal. Barnes prefers those then dead who had heard the gospel while living and become Christians, on three grounds, the natural meaning of the word, its use in the previous verse, and the fitness of the thought for readers under persecution; Ellicott refers the verse to Christ's descent and to the teaching of the third chapter; Clarke prefers the antediluvians preached to by Noah; Barnes also reports the martyrs and the sinners of the old world as further candidates.

Whether the English version can be trusted here. Ellicott says it is misleading and seems one of the rare cases where the original has been expanded by the translators for doctrinal ends, the Greek being simply, to the dead also; Clarke reports that there are as many translations of the verse as there are translators, and sets out three; the others translate without comment.

What the two closing clauses contrast. Barnes sets the treatment received from men against the treatment received from God, condemnation in the flesh against life in the spirit; Calvin takes judged as condemned and holds that the dead cease not to live with God in their spirit because Christ quickens them; Robertson marks the opposition of the two prepositional phrases; Wesley calls the judgment rash and unrighteous.
outliers: Calvin alone draws a consequence for the reader's own death, arguing that since the grace of Christ once penetrated to the dead we shall partake of it when dead, and that we set limits much too narrow to it if we confine it to the present life.
Gill alone insists that the opening words look forward rather than back, and that what follows gives not the reason of the preaching but the event consequent upon it.
themes: the gospel preached to the dead

7.pericope_label: But the end of all things is at hand: be ye therefore sober, and watch unto prayer.

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin allow the several ends and defend the nearness. Gill says that with respect to particular persons the end of life, which is the end of all things in this world to a man, is near at hand, being but as a hand's breadth, passing away like a tale that is told and appearing as a vapour for a while and then vanishing away. Or this may be said with regard to the Jews, the end of their church and civil state being near at hand, of their sacrifices, temple, city and nation; or with respect to the whole universe, to the scheme and fashion of this world, which will soon be gone though the substance will abide, when the heavens shall pass away and the earth and all therein will be burnt up; when there will be an end of all the purposes and promises of God respecting the present state of things concerning his church and people, and of the judgments of God upon his enemies here, when the man of sin will be destroyed and the wickedness of the wicked will have come to an end, and with it the sorrows, afflictions and persecutions of the saints. Calvin says that though the faithful hear that their felicity is elsewhere than in the world, yet, as they think they should live long, this false thought renders them careless and even slothful, so that they direct not their thoughts to the kingdom of God; hence the Apostle, to rouse them from the drowsiness of the flesh, reminds them that the end of all things was nigh, intimating that we ought not to sit still in the world from which we must soon remove. He does not speak only of the end of individuals, but of the universal renovation of the world, as though he had said that Christ will shortly come who will put an end to all things. It is no wonder, Calvin says, that the cares of this world overwhelm us and make us drowsy, if the view of present things dazzles our eyes, for we promise almost all of us an eternity to ourselves in this world, or at least the end never comes to our mind; but were the trumpet of Christ to sound in our ears it would powerfully rouse us and not suffer us to lie torpid. It may be objected, he continues, that a long series of ages has passed away since Peter wrote this and yet the end is not come; and his reply is that the time seems long to us because we measure its length by the spaces of this fleeting life, but if we could understand the perpetuity of future life many ages would appear to us like a moment. We must remember this principle, Calvin adds, that from the time when Christ once appeared there is nothing left for the faithful but with suspended minds ever to look forward to his second coming. There is no ground to suppose, as some have supposed, that the end of all things was the end of the Jews as a nation, the destruction of the temple and its worship, and it is strange that such a notion should be entertained, especially when the Apostle refers to the same subject in his Second Epistle, where the end of the world is plainly spoken of. The sobriety and the watching to which he exhorted them belong, as Calvin thinks, to the mind rather than to the body, the words being similar to those of Christ about watching because we know neither the day nor the hour; for as an indulgence in surfeiting and sleep renders the body unfit for its duties, so the vain cares and pleasures of the world inebriate the mind and render it drowsy. By adding prayer he points out an exercise especially necessary, in which the faithful ought to be particularly occupied, since their whole strength depends on the Lord.

Henry states the position and draws the inference. The miserable destruction of the Jewish church and nation foretold by our Saviour is now very near, and consequently the time of their persecution and of the readers' sufferings is but very short; their own life and that of their enemies will soon come to its utmost period; nay, the world itself will not continue very long, since the conflagration will put an end to it and all things must be swallowed up in an endless eternity. The inference comprises a series of exhortations, of which the first is to sobriety and watchfulness: let the frame and temper of your minds be grave, stayed and solid, and observe strict temperance and sobriety in the use of all worldly enjoyments; do not suffer yourselves to be caught with your former sins and temptations, and watch unto prayer, taking care to be continually in a calm sober disposition fit for prayer and frequent in prayers, lest this end come upon you unawares. Henry draws three lessons. The consideration of our approaching end is a powerful argument to make us sober in all worldly matters and earnest in religious affairs. Those who would pray to purpose must watch unto prayer, watching over their own spirits, watching all fit opportunities, and doing their duty in the best manner they can. And the right ordering of the body is of great use to promote the good of the soul, for when the appetites and inclinations of the body are restrained and governed by God's word and true reason, and the interests of the body are submitted to the interests and necessities of the soul, then it is not the soul's enemy but its friend and helper.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson weigh the nearness and the imperatives. Barnes says the declaration is designed to support and encourage them in their trials and to excite them to lead a holy life by the assurance that the end of all things was drawing nigh. The phrase would naturally refer to the end of the world, the winding up of human affairs, but it is not absolutely certain that the apostle used it here in that sense: it might mean that so far as they were concerned the end of all things drew near, since death is to each one the end of all things here below, the end of his plans and of his interest in all that pertains to sublunary affairs. Even if the phrase referred originally to the end of the world, Barnes says, it is probable that it would soon come to denote the end of life in relation to the affairs of each individual, since if it was believed that the end of the world was near it must consequently be believed that the earthly career of each one drew near to a close; and it is possible that the latter signification came ultimately to predominate. The word rendered is at hand may refer either to proximity of place or of time, and always denotes that the place or the time referred to was not far off; Barnes lists its uses in both senses, and concludes that as applied to time or to an approaching event the idea is undoubtedly that it is close by and will soon occur. If this refers to the end of the world it would mean that it was soon to occur; if to death, that this was an event which could not be far distant, perhaps an event to be hastened by their trials. Ellicott renders it, hath come nigh, the same word as in Matthew, and calls it but a repetition in other words of the fifth verse, inserted again to give weight to all the exhortations which follow. Probably, he says, if Peter had thought the world would stand twenty centuries more he would have expressed himself differently. The two imperatives, Ellicott says, sum up the cautions given in the opening verses before passing on to the next subject: the first verb includes more than sobriety and means the keeping of a check upon all the desires, while the usual notion of sobriety is more exactly conveyed in the word rendered watch, which is the same as earlier in the letter. Unto prayer, he adds, is a slip for unto prayers, the difference being that it does not mean we are to be always in a frame to pray, but that actual prayers should always be on our lips, every incident in life suggesting them; they would be especially necessary if any moment might see the end of the world. The tense of the imperatives in the Greek carries out the notion that the persons addressed had slipped into a careless state from which they needed an arousal. Robertson parses the perfect active indicative of the verb to draw near, the same form used by the Baptist of the Messiah's arrival and by James of the second coming. How near, he says, Peter does not say, but he urges readiness as Jesus did and as Paul did, though it is drawing nearer all the time, but not at once. The first imperative is a first aorist ingressive from the words for sound and mind, so that it means, be ye of sound mind, in view of the coming of Christ; the second is likewise ingressive, and the noun for prayers is plural.

Clarke and Wesley refer the end to Jerusalem and join the three duties. Clarke thinks that here also Peter keeps the history of the deluge before his eyes, finding a parallel to the state of the Jews in his own time in that of the antediluvians in the days of Noah, since God said to Noah that the end of all flesh was come before him, and this was spoken at a time when God had decreed the destruction of the world by a flood. Peter says the end of all things is at hand, and this he spoke when God had determined to destroy the Jewish people and their polity by one of the most signal judgments that ever fell upon any nation; in a very few years after the epistle was written, even taking the lowest computation, Jerusalem was destroyed by the Romans. To this destruction, which was literally then at hand, the apostle alludes: the end of the temple, the end of the Levitical priesthood, the end of the whole Jewish economy was then at hand. If the words could be taken in any general sense, Clarke adds, then we might say to every present generation that the end of all things is at hand, the end of all the good which the wicked enjoy and the end of all the evil which the righteous suffer. To be sober is to make a prudent and moderate use of all one possesses, and to watch against all occasions of sin, and to pray for the supporting hand of God, that they might escape the destruction coming upon the Jews and be saved from among them when the scourge came. Wesley says the end of all things is the end of their wrongs and of the readers' sufferings, and states the connection between the duties: temperance helps watchfulness, and both of them help prayer, so watch that ye may pray, and pray that ye may watch.

debates: What end is meant. Clarke takes it of the destruction of Jerusalem by the Romans, then a very few years off, and finds the apostle keeping the deluge in view since God used the same words to Noah; Henry takes that destruction first but adds their own lives and the world itself; Gill allows three senses together, the end of each man's life, the end of the Jewish church and state, and the end of the frame of this world; Calvin refuses the national reading outright as having no ground, and takes the words of the universal renovation of the world.

How near the end is. Barnes traces the verb through its uses of nearness in place and time and concludes it means close by, while allowing that death may be the end intended for each man; Robertson says how near the apostle does not say, and that it draws nearer all the time yet is not at once; Ellicott says frankly that if Peter had thought the world would stand twenty centuries more he would have expressed himself differently; Calvin answers the same objection by measuring time against the perpetuity of the life to come, in which many ages appear a moment.

Whether the sobriety is of body or of mind. Calvin assigns both words to the mind rather than the body, since the cares and pleasures of the world inebriate the mind as surfeiting unfits the body; Henry takes the body seriously in its own right, holding that its right ordering promotes the good of the soul and makes it the soul's friend and helper rather than its enemy; Clarke makes it a prudent and moderate use of all one possesses; Ellicott says the first verb means keeping a check on all the desires and that the usual notion of sobriety belongs rather to the second.
outliers: Ellicott alone corrects the number of the noun, holding that unto prayer is a slip for unto prayers, so that the apostle asks not for a standing frame of mind fit to pray but for actual prayers always on the lips, suggested by every incident of life.

Calvin alone treats the long delay since the letter was written as an objection to be answered rather than a difficulty to be conceded, replying that we measure time by the spaces of this fleeting life and that against the perpetuity of the life to come many ages appear a moment.

8.pericope_label: And above all things have fervent charity among yourselves: for charity shall cover the multitude of sins.

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin widen the circle and defend the number. Gill says that charity or love is to be exercised towards all men, even towards enemies, but more especially towards the saints, and that under such a consideration in which it cannot be exercised towards others, namely as their brethren in Christ, as the children of God, as redeemed by Christ and sanctified by the Spirit; and these not only such as are of the same nation and belong to the same particular church and community, or of the same denomination, but all the saints everywhere, whether Jews or Gentiles, or of whatsoever name, and in whatsoever state and condition. This love ought to be mutual and reciprocal, and to be warm and fervent, and not lukewarm and indifferent as it too often is, and should be constant and perpetual, as the Vulgate Latin and Arabic versions here read. The apostle exhorts to this above all things else, Gill says, since outward sobriety, and watchings, and prayer, and all other duties, are nothing without it, this being the sum and substance of the law and the fulfilling of it. Calvin commends charity or love as the first thing, for it is the bond of perfection, and bids it to be intense or vehement, which is the same thing, for whosoever is immoderately fervent in self-love loves others coldly. He commends it on account of its fruit, because it buries innumerable sins, than which nothing is more desirable. The sentence is taken from Solomon, whose words are that hatred discovers reproaches but love covers a multitude of sins, and what Solomon meant is sufficiently clear, for the two clauses contain things set in contrast one with the other: as he says in the first clause that hatred is the cause why men traduce and defame one another and spread whatever is reproachful and dishonourable, so it follows that a contrary effect is ascribed to love, that men who love one another kindly and courteously forgive one another, whence it comes that, willingly burying each other's vices, one seeks to preserve the honour of another. The quotation, Calvin notes, is from the Hebrew, and the sentence in the Greek version is evidently different, the same words being found also in James. Thus Peter confirms his exhortation, that nothing is more necessary than to cherish mutual love; for who is there that has not many faults? All therefore stand in need of forgiveness, and there is no one who does not wish to be forgiven, and this singular benefit love brings to us when it exists among us, so that innumerable evils are covered in oblivion; whereas where loose reins are given to hatred, men by mutual biting and tearing must necessarily consume one another, as Paul says. It ought to be noticed, Calvin adds, that Solomon does not say that only a few sins are covered but a multitude, according to what Christ declares when he bids us forgive our brethren seventy times seven; and the more sins love covers, the more evident appears its usefulness for the wellbeing of mankind. It hence appears, he concludes, how absurd are the Papists, who seek to elicit from this passage their own satisfactions.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson define the word and place the quotation. Barnes says the phrase above all things means more than all things else, and that fervent charity is warm, ardent love towards each other, the word rendered fervent meaning properly extended, then intent, earnest, fervent. The saying that charity shall cover a multitude of sins he takes to mean that love to another shall so cover or hide a great many imperfections in him that we shall not notice them, and quotes it as taken from Proverbs 10:12, that love covereth all sins. For the truth of it, he says, we have only to appeal to the experience of every one: true love to another makes us kind to his imperfections, charitable towards his faults, and often blind even to the existence of faults, since we would not see the imperfections of those whom we love, and our attachment for what we esteem their real excellencies makes us insensible to their errors; and if we love them we are ready to cover over their faults, even those which we may see in them. Barnes quotes the Christian poet that love is gentle, delicate and kind, to faults compassionate or blind. The passage, he says, is not the same in signification as that in James 5:20, which means that by the conversion of another the sins of him who is converted shall be covered over, or not brought to judgment, so far as God is concerned, whereas this passage means that under the influence of love the sins of another shall be covered over so far as we are concerned, that is, they shall be unobserved or forgiven. The language does not mean, as the Romanists maintain, that charity shall procure us pardon for a multitude of sins; for besides that such a doctrine is contrary to the uniform teachings of the Scriptures elsewhere, it is a departure from the obvious meaning of the passage, the subject on which the apostle is treating being the advantage of love in our conduct towards others. Ellicott says the original is far more vigorous: but before all things keeping intense your charity towards yourselves. Peter assumes that the charity is there, but insists on its not being suffered to flag in outward expression. On the verb he notes that the right reading is neither shall nor will but the present, covereth. The words are usually said to be a quotation from Proverbs 10:12, that hatred stirreth up strifes but love covereth all sins; but they are widely different from the Greek version in that passage and also vary from the Hebrew, and as precisely the same variation occurs in James 5:20, it seems more probable either that Peter had the passage of James consciously in his mind, or that the proverb was current and familiar to both writers in the form, love covereth a multitude of sins. It is therefore unsafe, Ellicott says, to argue from the exact shade of meaning which the words bear in Proverbs. To cover, in Hebrew, often means to forgive, the idea being that of an offensive object which you bury or hide by putting something else over it; and the place in Proverbs seems to mean that whereas a bitter enemy will rake up every old grudge again and again, one who loves will not allow even himself to see the wrongs done to him by a friend. If this sense be accepted here it will imply that the Christians in Asia had a good deal to put up with from each other; but even so the argument seems a little strained, and it far better suits the context to take the proverb in the same sense as in James, without any reference to the Old Testament passage. Robertson notes the phrase above all things as occurring also in James, and parses the present active participle with the predicate accusative of an adjective from a verb meaning to stretch out, so that it means holding intent your love among yourselves; the adjective occurs only here in the New Testament. On the covering he refers to James for the meaning, and states it in a phrase: the sins of the one loved, not of the one loving.

Clarke and Wesley describe what the covering looks like. Clarke renders the phrase intense love, and says that a loving disposition leads us to pass by the faults of others, to forgive offences against ourselves, and to excuse and lessen, as far as is consistent with truth, the transgressions of men; it does not mean, he insists, that our love to others will induce God to pardon our offences. Wesley says that love covereth all things: he that loves another covers his faults, how many soever they be, turns away his own eyes from them, and as far as is possible hides them from others; and he continually prays that all the sinner's iniquities may be forgiven and his sins covered, while meantime the God of love measures to him with the same measure into his bosom.

debates: Whether the saying is a quotation from Proverbs. Barnes and Calvin take it so, Calvin expounding the original from its two contrasted clauses and noting that the quotation follows the Hebrew rather than the Greek version; Ellicott doubts it, since the words differ widely from that version and vary from the Hebrew too, and since the same variation appears in James, and holds it likelier that the proverb was current and familiar to both writers, so that it is unsafe to argue from the shade of meaning the words bear in Proverbs.

Whose sins are covered. Robertson settles it in a phrase, the sins of the one loved and not of the one loving; Barnes says love makes us kind to another's imperfections and often blind to their existence; Clarke says it leads us to pass by the faults of others and excuse their transgressions as far as truth allows; Wesley adds that the lover prays for the sinner's forgiveness and is measured to with the same measure.

Whether charity procures pardon for the one who shows it. Barnes denies the Romanist reading as contrary both to the uniform teaching of Scripture and to the obvious meaning of the place; Clarke denies flatly that our love to others will induce God to pardon our offences; Calvin says it appears from this how absurd are those who elicit their own satisfactions from the verse; Barnes further distinguishes the saying in James, which he takes of sins covered so far as God is concerned.
outliers: Calvin alone explains the strength of the word from its opposite, holding that the love is bidden to be intense because whoever is immoderately fervent in self-love loves others coldly.
Ellicott alone treats the saying as a floating proverb rather than a citation, and draws the methodological consequence that the sense it bears in Proverbs cannot be used to fix its sense here.

9.pericope_label: Use hospitality one to another without grudging. As every man hath received the gift, even so minister the same one to another, as good stewards of the manifold grace of God.

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin describe the duty and the design of the diversity. Gill renders the word, be lovers of strangers, that is, such as are of a distant country or come from afar and are unknown by face, especially good men obliged to remove from their native country for the sake of religion or by one providence or another; these are to be loved, and love is to be shown them both negatively, by not vexing them and making them uneasy in body or mind, by not oppressing them by violence and injustice or making exorbitant demands upon them, or perverting judgment with respect to them, and positively, by directing, counselling and advising them, and if need be by giving them food and raiment and lodging. It is what men have been led to by the very light of nature, Gill says, as in the instances of Jethro the Midianite towards Moses and the inhabitants of Melita towards Paul and his company, and is what God enjoined the Israelites by divers laws, since they had been strangers in the land of Egypt. On the next verse Gill says this is a general rule laid down by the apostle, according to which distribution of every kind, whether in things temporal or spiritual, is to be made, even according to the nature, quality and quantity of the gift received. The greatest gift God bestows on men in this life is special grace, which God gives of his sovereign will and pleasure, liberally and abundantly, without the deserts of men, of which kind are faith, repentance, hope and love; the next to this is the ministerial gift, or what qualifies men for the work of the ministry, which is not anything in nature nor acquired by art and industry but a gift of grace bestowed on some in a higher and on others in a lower degree; and besides these there are the gifts of nature and providence, as human wisdom and the knowledge of things natural and civil, riches and wealth, and the various good things of life. Calvin says that after having generally exhorted them to love one another the apostle specially mentions one of the duties of love: at that time hospitality was commonly used and was deemed in a manner a sacred kind of humanity, and he bids them mutually to exercise it, so that no one might require more from others than what he himself was prepared to render. It is a rare example, Calvin adds, that one spends himself and his own on his neighbour without any disparaging reflection, and the Apostle would have us show kindness willingly and with a cheerful mind. On the next verse he says the apostle reminds us what we ought to bear in mind when we do good to our neighbours, for nothing is more fitted to correct our murmurings than to remember that we do not give our own but only dispense what God has committed to us. When he says, minister the gift which every one has received, he intimates that to each had been distributed what they had on this condition, that in helping their brethren they might be the ministers of God; and the second clause explains the first, since instead of ministry he mentions stewardship, and for the gift received he mentions the manifold graces which God variously distributes, so that each might confer in common his own portion. If then we excel others in any gift, Calvin says, let us remember that we are as to this the stewards of God, in order that we may kindly impart it to our neighbours as their necessity or benefit may require.
