But this consideration is also very important, that the Lord has so divided his manifold graces that no one is to be content with one thing and with his own gifts, but every one has need of the help and aid of his brother; this is a bond which God has appointed for retaining friendship among men, for they cannot live without mutual assistance, so that he who in many things seeks the aid of his brethren ought to communicate more freely what he has received. This bond of unity has been observed and noticed by heathens, but Peter teaches us that God had designedly done this, that he might bind men one to another.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson take the duty, the gift and the stewardship. Barnes says the Greek for without grudging is without murmurs, that is, without complaining of the hardship of doing it, of the time and expense and trouble required; the idea of grudging in the common sense of that word, of doing it unwillingly or regretting the expense and considering it as ill bestowed, is not exactly the idea here, but that we are to do it without murmuring or complaining. It greatly enhances the value of hospitality that it be done on our part with entire cheerfulness, since one of the duties involved is to make a guest happy, and this can be done in no other way than by showing him that he is welcome. On the next verse Barnes says the word rendered the gift means endowment of any kind, but especially that conferred by the Holy Spirit, and here seems to refer to every kind of endowment by which we can do good to others, especially every kind of qualification furnished by religion; it does not refer particularly to the ministry of the word, though it is applicable to that and includes it, but to all the gifts and graces by which we can contribute to the welfare of others, all of which is regarded as a gift of God and not owing to ourselves. To minister would refer to any kind of ministering, whether by counsel, by advice, by the supply of the wants of the poor, or by preaching, and means that in whatever God has favoured us more than others we should be ready to minister to their wants. As good stewards means regarding ourselves as the mere stewards of God, appointed by him to do this work for him and entrusted by him with what is needful to benefit others; he intends to do them good, but means to do it through our instrumentality, and has entrusted to us as stewards what he designed to confer on them. The manifold grace of God is the grace or favour of God evinced in many ways, or by a variety of gifts. Ellicott says it is a great pity that here again the participial clauses are broken up in our version into separate injunctions, since properly it is, being hospitable; this is the first form of charity, the receiving of Christians who came from other towns, and he notes how such hospitality covers, to the surprise of the bestowers, a multitude of sins in the parable of the sheep and the goats. Without grudging means without murmuring, and Ellicott exclaims how frequently Christian hospitality is marred by grumbling at the expense and the trouble which it costs. On the next verse he notes that there is no definite article in the Greek, which might be rendered, according as every man was gifted; they are reminded, as in 1 Corinthians 4:7, that the gift was received and for the same purpose. At what period these gifts were received it is hard to say, since in some instances the gift was of a spiritual nature and in others of a temporal, but each has a gift of some kind for the benefit of the community. In the original the next word is ministering, and it is still an exhibition of the intense charity of the eighth verse. No one receives these gifts, spiritual or temporal, as his own; he is but a steward, and when he offers them to the Church it is not as a benefactor but as a servant, ministering. Grace, Ellicott says, is here used not in its theological sense but in the sense of bountiful giving, and the beautiful word rendered manifold brings out the subtle and picturesque variety with which God arranges and distributes his bounty; but the emphatic word of the sentence is of God. Robertson glosses the word for hospitality as friendly to strangers, an old word occurring in the New Testament only here and in the Pastoral Epistles, and notes that there is no verb in the Greek. Without murmuring answers to the phrase in Philippians, and complaint, he says, spoils hospitality; Jesus enjoined the entertainment of strangers, inns were rare and very poor, and hospitality made mission work possible. On the next verse Robertson calls the word for gift a late New Testament word from a verb meaning to give graciously, used here by Peter as one of the gifts of the Holy Spirit; ministering is a present active participle in the plural though the word for each is singular; and for steward, a house-manager, he compares its use of Paul himself and of any bishop, though here it is used of any Christian. The word rendered manifold means many-coloured.

Clarke and Wesley put the duty briefly and take the gift widely. Clarke says to use hospitality is to be ever ready to divide one's bread with the hungry and to succour the stranger, and that without grudging means without grumblings: nothing is to be done merely because it is commanded, but from love to God and man, and then it will be without grumbling. On the next verse Clarke says the word means a gift, any blessing of providence or grace, and that he cannot think it means here the Holy Ghost or any of his supernatural gifts or influences; it may include those, but it signifies anything given by the mere mercy and bounty of God, though perhaps in this place it may signify some or any office in the Church, a sense which the connection seems to require. Whatever gifts or endowments any man may possess, Clarke adds, they are properly speaking not his own but the Lord's property, to be employed in his work and to promote his glory. Wesley says the hospitality is to be shown by those who are of different towns or countries, and that without murmuring means with all cheerfulness. On the next verse he says the gift may be spiritual or temporal, ordinary or extraordinary, although the latter seems primarily intended, and that to minister it one to another is to employ it for the common good, as good stewards of the talents wherewith God's free love has entrusted us.

debates: What the gift is. Robertson takes it as one of the gifts of the Holy Spirit; Clarke says he cannot think the word means the Holy Ghost or his supernatural gifts here, though it may include them, and suspects it means some office in the Church; Barnes takes it as endowment of any kind, especially that conferred by the Spirit, and here as every endowment by which we can do good to others; Wesley allows spiritual or temporal, ordinary or extraordinary, but thinks the extraordinary primarily intended; Gill sorts them into special grace, the ministerial gift, and the gifts of nature and providence.

What the added words forbid. Barnes says the idea of grudging in the common sense, of doing a thing unwillingly or regretting the expense, is not exactly the idea, the Greek being without murmurs; Ellicott turns it into a rebuke of grumbling at the expense and trouble; Robertson says complaint spoils hospitality; Clarke says nothing should be done merely because commanded, but from love, and then it will be without grumbling.

Why the graces are various. Calvin holds the diversity deliberate, since the Lord so divided his gifts that no one is content with his own but each needs his brother's help, a bond heathens have noticed but which God appointed on purpose to bind men together; Ellicott finds in the word rendered manifold the subtle and picturesque variety with which God distributes his bounty, and says the emphatic word is of God; Robertson glosses it simply as many-coloured.
outliers: Ellicott alone binds the verse back to the one before it, making hospitality the first form of the intense charity there commanded and pointing to the parable where such hospitality covers a multitude of sins to the surprise of those who showed it.
Robertson alone supplies the circumstance that made the duty urgent, that inns were rare and very poor, so that hospitality was what made mission work possible.
themes: as every man hath received the gift

11.pericope_label: If any man speak, let him speak as the oracles of God; if any man minister, let him do it as of the ability which God giveth: that God in all things may be glorified through Jesus Christ, to whom be praise and dominion for ever and ever. Amen.

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin define the oracles and press the charge on teachers. Gill says this is an application of the general rule to a particular case, the public ministry of the word: if any man speak, not in any manner or on any subject, not in a private way or about things natural and civil, but in public and concerning divine things, let him speak as the oracles of God. By these, Gill says, are meant the writings of the Old Testament, the sacred Scriptures, so called because they come from God, are breathed and spoken by him, contain his mind and will, and are authoritative and infallible; and according to these he is to speak who speaks in public on divine subjects, both as to the matter and manner of his speech, the matter being agreeable to the divinely inspired word, fetched out of it and confirmed by it. Calvin says that as the apostle had spoken of the right and faithful use of gifts, he specifies two things as examples, and has chosen the most renowned. The office of teaching in the Church is a remarkable instance of God's favour, and he expressly commands those called to this office to act faithfully, speaking not only of what we owe to men but of what we owe to God, that we may not deprive him of his glory. He who speaks, that is, who is rightly appointed by public authority, is to perform reverently in God's fear and in sincerity the charge committed to him, regarding himself as engaged in God's work and as ministering God's word and not his own. Truly, Calvin says, were all those who profess to be teachers in the Church duly to consider this one thing, there would be in them much more fidelity and devotedness; for how great a thing is this, that in teaching the oracles of God they are representatives of Christ. Hence comes so much carelessness and rashness, because the sacred majesty of God's word is not borne in mind but by a few, and so they indulge themselves as in a worldly stewardship. We learn from these words, he adds, that it is not lawful for those engaged in teaching to do anything else but faithfully to deliver to others, as from hand to hand, the doctrine received from God; for the apostle forbids any one to go forth except he who is instructed in God's word and who proclaims infallible oracles as it were from his mouth, and therefore leaves no room for human inventions, briefly defining the doctrine which ought to be taught in the Church. Nor is the particle of similitude introduced here for the purpose of modifying the sentence, Calvin insists, as though it were sufficient to profess that it is God's word that is taught; this was commonly the case formerly with false prophets, and we see at this day how arrogantly men cover with this pretence their impious traditions.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson define the two offices and the doxology. Barnes takes the speaking as that of a preacher, referring here particularly to the office of the ministry, and says he is to speak as the oracles of God speak, in accordance with the truth which God has revealed and with an impressive sense of the responsibility of delivering a message from him; the word rendered oracles means properly something spoken or uttered, and then anything uttered by God, a divine communication or revelation. The word rendered minister may refer either to the office of a deacon or to any service which one renders to another, and commonly refers to service in general, to attendance on another or aid rendered to another, or to the distribution of alms. It seems probable, Barnes says, that the word here does not refer to the office of a deacon as such, because the peculiarity of that office was to take charge of the poor of the church and of the funds provided for them, whereas the apostle says that those to whom he referred should minister as of the ability which God giveth, which seems to imply that it was rather to distribute what was their own than what was committed to them by the church; the word may therefore refer to any aid we render to others in the church. As of the ability which God giveth is in regard to property, talent, strength and influence, and this is the limit of all obligation: no one is bound to go beyond his ability, and every one is required to come up to it. That God may be glorified is that he may be honoured by our doing all the good we can to others and thus showing the power of his religion, and through Jesus Christ means as the medium through whom all those holy influences come by which God is honoured. Ellicott says the apostle proceeds to speak of two particular forms taken by the manifold grace of God, the power to speak and the power to minister. The speaking is public preaching in the Church, and the man who does so is to do it as oracles of God; but the article is not added in the Greek, so that it must not be pressed to mean speaking on the model, or in accordance with the doctrines, of the Old Testament. Rather the emphatic word is of God, and the Apostle means that the preacher is not to trust to his own natural powers and wit, or to seek applause for himself, but to act as one possessed of powers not his own, to speak only that which God inspires him to speak. This clause, Ellicott says, must not be taken as complete in itself in this place: it is apparently only introduced to give point to what follows, the intention of the whole paragraph being to enforce liberality, since it is easy to recognise in spiritual things the principle of God being all in all, and Peter bids them apply the same principle to material gifts. Recollect, he paraphrases, that whatever you possess, you possess from God in trust for the Church; just as the man who preaches is to preach as a mere mouthpiece of God, so the man who gives must consider himself as being but God's dispenser, that in this too God may have all the glory. If any man minister does not mean ministering in the congregation or spiritual ministrations of any sort, Ellicott insists, but giving the good things of this life for the benefit of the poor: the word rendered ability not unfrequently expresses, like our word resources, a sufficiency of wealth, and the word which appears as giveth is the same used of supplying material blessings in 2 Corinthians 9:10, its original classical meaning being to pay the expenses of putting a play on the stage, which at Athens was a public burden borne by the wealthier citizens in turn, like the shrievalty of an English county. Robertson takes both clauses as conditions of the first class, assumed as fact, and notes that there is no predicate in the conclusion of the first, so that the verb has to be supplied. The phrase oracles of God is used elsewhere of the Mosaic law, of the Old Testament and of the substance of Christian teaching, and here of the utterances of God through Christian teachers, the noun being a diminutive of the word for speech. The relative in the clause about ability is attracted from the accusative, and the verb, an old one from the word for a chorus leader, occurs in the New Testament only here and at 2 Corinthians 9:10: God, Robertson says, is the supplier of strength. On the doxology he notes that the phrase means, to whom is, that is to Jesus Christ, the immediate antecedent, though in Romans and Jude the doxology is to God through Christ; he lists many other doxologies, and observes that the others addressed to Christ are few.

Clarke and Wesley apply the rule to preachers and to givers. Clarke says that in order to explain or enforce God's word and edify his neighbour, let a man do it as those did to whom the living oracles were committed, who spoke as they were inspired by the Holy Ghost; those, therefore, at Pontus and elsewhere who undertook to teach others should speak by the same influence, or, if not under this immediate influence, should speak as or according to the oracles already delivered, grounding all their exhortations and doctrines on some portion of that revelation already given. This command, Clarke says, is sent to every man upon earth in holy orders, in pretended holy orders, or pretending to holy orders, and their teaching should be what the oracles of God, the Holy Scriptures, teach and authenticate. Perhaps the ministering here, he adds, may refer to the care of the poor, and the ability is the quantum of means which God may have placed in their hands; and they are to minister this as coming immediately from God, and lead the minds of the poor to consider him as their benefactor, that he in all things may be glorified through Christ Jesus. This is implied in the essence of any charitable act: the actor is not the author, God is the author, and the poor man should be taught to consider him as his immediate benefactor; those who give anything as from themselves rob God, for to him the praise for all good and the dominion over all men and things belong for ever. Wesley says that if any man speak, let him speak in his whole conversation, public and private, as the oracles of God, letting all his words be according to this pattern both as to matter and manner, and more especially in public. By this mark, Wesley says, we may always know who are so far the true or false prophets: the oracles of God teach that men should repent, believe, obey; and he that treats of faith and leaves out repentance, or does not enjoin practical holiness to believers, does not speak as the oracles of God and does not preach Christ, let him think as highly of himself as he will. If any man minister, that is, serve his brother in love, whether in spirituals or temporals, let him minister as of the ability which God giveth, humbly and diligently, ascribing all his power to God and using it with his might; and the glory is of God's wisdom, which teaches us to speak, and the might is what enables us to act.

debates: What the oracles of God are. Gill takes them for the writings of the Old Testament, so that the preacher's matter must be fetched out of them and confirmed by them; Ellicott refuses that on the ground that the article is not in the Greek, and makes the emphatic word of God, so that the preacher is to act as one possessed of powers not his own; Robertson notes that the phrase is used elsewhere of the Mosaic law, of the Old Testament and of Christian teaching, and takes it here of the utterances of God through Christian teachers; Clarke allows either the immediate influence or the revelation already given.

What the ministering is. Barnes allows that the word might mean the office of a deacon but thinks it does not, since that office had charge of the church's funds while the apostle's words about ability imply the distributing of a man's own; Ellicott says flatly that it is not spiritual service of any sort but the giving of this life's good things to the poor, and takes ability in the sense of resources; Clarke agrees that it is the care of the poor; Robertson takes the same verb to mean that God is the supplier of strength.

How much weight the particle of comparison carries. Calvin refuses to let it soften the charge, holding that it is not enough to profess that what is taught is God's word, as the false prophets did, and that the apostle leaves no room for human inventions; Ellicott makes the phrase a claim that the preacher speaks only what God inspires him to speak; Wesley turns it into a test of true and false prophets.
outliers: Ellicott alone reads the whole paragraph as one argument for liberality, holding that the clause about preaching is not complete in itself but introduced to give point to the giving, so that as the preacher is a mere mouthpiece of God the giver is but God's dispenser.

Ellicott alone traces the verb rendered giveth to the classical burden of paying the expenses of putting a play on the stage, which at Athens fell on the wealthier citizens in turn; Robertson takes the same word to its root in the chorus leader but draws from it that God supplies strength rather than that the giver supplies wealth.
themes: speak as the oracles of God

12.pericope_label: Beloved, think it not strange concerning the fiery trial which is to try you, as though some strange thing happened unto you; but rejoice, inasmuch as ye are partakers of Christ's sufferings; that, when his glory shall be revealed, ye may be glad also with exceeding joy.

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin explain the figure and the fellowship. Gill says that by the fiery trial may be meant either the destruction of Jerusalem, which was at hand and of which the apostle may be giving the Jews he writes to notice beforehand, that they might be prepared for it and not be overwhelmed with consternation, since though in other countries they must be affected by it; or else the afflictions and persecutions which daily came upon them for the sake of Christ and his Gospel, signified by fire or burning because they are grievous to the flesh and give great uneasiness and pain to it, because the fury of men and the violence of their rage are expressed thereby, and because the people of God under them are sometimes ready to conceive that the wrath of God is poured out like fire upon them. The apostle would not have them entertain any such thoughts, Gill says, and therefore calls them beloved, that is, of God, as they were notwithstanding all the fiery trials brought upon them. On the next verse Gill says they are partakers not of Christ's personal sufferings, though they are partakers of the benefits and blessings which come through them, such as justification, peace and pardon, but of the sufferings of his body the church, which is mystically himself; these are called his because of the union between him and his people, and because of the sympathy he bears to them, and because they are endured for the sake of him and his Gospel, and conform the saints and make them like unto him. Suffering saints should therefore rejoice in this, that their sufferings are accounted by Christ as his own, who in all their afflictions is afflicted, and that they are honoured to suffer for his name's sake. Calvin says there is frequent mention of afflictions in this Epistle, but that here the apostle speaks not of troubles common to man's life but of wrongs done to the faithful for the name of Christ. First he reminded them that they ought not to have deemed it strange as a thing sudden and unexpected, by which he intimates that they ought by long meditation to have been previously prepared to bear the cross; for whosoever has resolved to fight under Christ's banner will not be dismayed when persecution happens, but, as one accustomed to it, will patiently bear it. That we may be in a prepared state of mind when the waves of persecution roll over us, Calvin says, we ought in due time to habituate ourselves to such an event by meditating continually on the cross. He proves that the cross is useful to us by two arguments, that God thus tries our faith and that we become thus partakers with Christ; the trial of our faith is most necessary and we ought willingly to obey God who provides for our salvation, but the chief consolation is to be derived from fellowship with Christ. It is indeed a cause of joy when God tries our faith by persecution, but the other joy far surpasses it, when the Son of God allots to us the same course of life with himself, that he might lead us to a blessed participation of heavenly glory. The wicked also bear many afflictions, Calvin adds, but as they are separated from Christ they apprehend nothing but God's wrath and curse, so that sorrow and dread overwhelm them. Since this world is like a labyrinth in which no end of evils appears, the apostle refers to the future revelation of Christ's glory, as though he had said that the day of its revelation ought to be expected. He mentions a twofold joy, one which we now enjoy in hope and the other whose full fruition the coming of Christ shall bring; the first is mingled with grief and sorrow, the second is connected with exultation. For it is not suitable in the midst of afflictions to think of a joy which can free us from all trouble, but the consolations of God moderate evils, so that we can rejoice at the same time.

Henry says the frequent repetition of counsel and comfort to Christians considered as sufferers, in every chapter of this epistle, shows that the greatest danger these new converts were in arose from the persecutions to which their embracing Christianity exposed them. The good behaviour of Christians under sufferings is the most difficult part of their duty, but necessary both for the honour of Christ and their own comfort; and therefore the apostle, having exhorted them to the great duty of mortification, comes here to direct them in the necessary duty of patience under sufferings, since an unmortified spirit is very unfit to bear trials. Henry notes the apostle's kind manner of address to these poor despised Christians, that they were his beloved, and gives his advice: they should not think their sufferings strange nor be surprised at them as if some unexpected event befell them, for though they be sharp and fiery they are designed only to try, not to ruin them, to try their sincerity, strength, patience and trust in God. On the contrary they ought rather to rejoice under their sufferings, because theirs may properly be called Christ's sufferings, being of the same kind and for the same cause that Christ suffered; they make us conformable to him, he suffers in them and feels in our infirmities, and if we be partakers of his sufferings we shall also be made partakers of his glory. Henry draws three lessons. True Christians love and own the children of God in their lowest and most distressing circumstances, and never look more amiable one to another than in their adversities. There is no reason for Christians to think strange, or to wonder, at the unkindnesses and persecutions of the world, because they are forewarned of them, and Christ himself endured them. And Christians ought not only to be patient but to rejoice in their sharpest and sorest sufferings for Christ, because they are tokens of divine favour.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson date the trial and construe the joy. Barnes says they are not to consider it as anything they had no reason to expect, or as anything which may not happen to others also, and takes the fiery trial as referring doubtless to some severe persecution which was then impending, adding that we have not the means of determining precisely what this was. The word rendered fiery trial occurs only here and twice in the Revelation, where it is rendered burning; it means properly a being on fire, a burning or conflagration, and then any severe trial, so that it cannot be demonstrated from this word that they were literally to suffer by fire, though it is clear that some heavy calamity was before them. On the next verse Barnes says the sufferings are of the same kind that Christ endured, and inflicted for the same reasons, and that they were to regard it as a matter of rejoicing that they were identified with Christ even in suffering. When his glory shall be revealed refers to the day of judgment, and they shall be glad with exceeding joy on being admitted to the rewards he will then confer on his people. Every good man, Barnes adds, will have joy when immediately at death he is received into the presence of his Saviour, but his joy will be complete only when, in the presence of assembled worlds, he shall hear the sentence which shall confirm him in happiness for ever. Ellicott says the word rendered think it strange is the same as in the fourth verse and means literally to feel like people in a strange country, lost and bewildered, and is further explained by the clause about a strange thing happening; these Hebrew Christians felt at first that it was not what was to be expected, that those who attached themselves to the Messiah should have a life of sorrow and persecution in the world. The rendering of the next clause, he says, is not only slovenly but conveys a false impression, for the fiery trial was not future but actually present: literally it runs, be not bewildered at the conflagration among you taking place for a trial to you, so that already the Asiatic Christians are enduring a fierce persecution. On the next verse Ellicott says that rejoicing is the opposite of being bewildered at it, since rejoicing implies a recognition of its character and purpose; the word rendered inasmuch as seems to mean in proportion as, so that the more nearly you are made to share Christ's sufferings the more you should rejoice. He illustrates this from the Acts of Probus, a Cappadocian, where after many other tortures the judge ordered some nails to be heated and run through his hands, and the martyr exclaimed, Glory to Thee, Lord Jesus Christ, who hast even deigned to let my hands be pierced for Thy name's sake. The word rendered that means in order that, and is to be attached to the commands not to think it strange but to rejoice, so that at the revelation of his glory also, as now in the sharing of his sufferings, they may rejoice, exulting; such a recognition of the meaning of suffering, and such a rejoicing in suffering now, is a sure means to rejoicing in glory also hereafter. Robertson takes the prohibition with the present passive imperative, be not amazed, and calls the fiery trial the metaphorical sense of an old word used since Aristotle, from the verb to burn; it occurs in Proverbs for the smelting of gold and silver, and in the Psalms, where God is said to have smelted us as silver is smelted. The participle rendered which cometh upon you is present middle, already coming, and the phrase rendered to try you means for testing; the clause about a strange thing is a genitive absolute giving the alleged reason. On the next verse Robertson glosses the conjunction as in so far forth as, an old conjunction occurring in the New Testament only here and twice in Paul, and parses the present active indicative of the verb to share in, followed by the dative. The purpose clause has the second aorist passive subjunctive of the verb to rejoice with the present middle participle of the verb to exult, so that it means, that ye may rejoice exulting, the same idea being associated with the second coming in the first chapter.

Clarke and Wesley describe the burning and number the arguments. Clarke says the metaphor is old but noble, representing the Christians at Pontus as having fire cast upon them for the trying of their faith, as gold is tried by fire. Peter returns here, he says, to what he had often touched upon in this epistle, namely to exhort the Christians to behave with patience and integrity under their present severe persecution, and uses five arguments. First, he intimates that it was not a strange or unusual thing for the people of God to be persecuted. Secondly, that if they suffered here as Christ did they should hereafter be glorified with him. Thirdly, that besides the prospect of that future glory they had at present the Spirit of God for their support and comfort. Fourthly, that it was an honour for any of them to suffer, not as a malefactor, but as a Christian. Fifthly, that though the afflictions began with the Christians, yet the weight of the storm would fall upon the unbelievers. From these considerations, Clarke says, he exhorted them to persevere in their duty and trust all events with God. Wesley says that to wonder not at the burning which is among you is the literal meaning of the expression, and that it seems to include both martyrdom itself, which so frequently was by fire, and all the other sufferings joined with, or previous to, it, which is permitted by the wisdom of God for their trial. On the next verse he says that as they partake of the sufferings of Christ, while they suffer for his sake, they are to rejoice in hope of more abundant glory, for the measure of glory answers the measure of suffering, and much more abundantly.

debates: Whether the fiery trial is present or still to come. Ellicott calls the English rendering not only slovenly but false in the impression it gives, since the persecution was actually taking place, and would render it, be not bewildered at the conflagration among you; Robertson agrees, taking the participle as already coming; Barnes reads it of a persecution then impending and grants that we cannot determine precisely what it was.

What the figure of fire means. Clarke calls the metaphor old but noble and takes it of faith tried as gold is tried; Wesley thinks it includes martyrdom by fire itself as well as the sufferings before it; Gill explains it three ways, as grievous to the flesh, as expressing the fierceness of men's rage, and as what makes sufferers think God's wrath is poured out on them; Robertson traces the word to the smelting of gold and silver in the Old Testament.

Whose sufferings are shared. Gill says not Christ's personal sufferings, though the benefits of those are enjoyed, but the sufferings of his body the church, which is mystically himself; Barnes says sufferings of the same kind that he endured and inflicted for the same reasons; Calvin makes fellowship with Christ the chief consolation and distinguishes the afflictions of the wicked, who being separated from Christ apprehend nothing but wrath.

How the two joys stand to each other. Calvin distinguishes the joy now had in hope, mingled with grief, from the full fruition at Christ's coming, and warns that it is not suitable in affliction to think of a joy that frees us from all trouble, since the consolations of God only moderate our evils; Barnes distinguishes the joy of being received at death into the presence of the Saviour from the complete joy of the sentence before assembled worlds; Ellicott makes the present rejoicing itself the means to the future.
outliers: Ellicott alone measures the rejoicing against the suffering, taking the conjunction to mean in proportion as, and illustrates it from a martyr's act in which the sufferer thanked Christ for the privilege of having his hands pierced.
Clarke alone numbers the apostle's arguments, listing five, and ends with the observation that though the afflictions begin with the Christians the weight of the storm will fall upon the unbelievers.

14.pericope_label: If ye be reproached for the name of Christ, happy are ye; for the spirit of glory and of God resteth upon you: on their part he is evil spoken of, but on your part he is glorified. But let none of you suffer as a murderer, or as a thief, or as an evildoer, or as a busybody in other men's matters. Yet if any man suffer as a Christian, let him not be ashamed; but let him glorify God on this behalf.

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin weigh the reproach and the name. Gill says the reproach is for being called by Christ's name, for bearing the name of Christians, for believing in him and professing him, and for the sake of his Gospel, which is sometimes called his name; the apostle makes no doubt of it but supposes and takes for granted that they are and will be reproached, and yet pronounces them blessed persons. On the last verse Gill notes that the name Christian was first given to the disciples at Antioch, either by themselves or by the Gentiles, and, being agreeable to them, was retained. Calvin says the apostle mentions reproaches because there is often more bitterness in them than in the loss of goods or in the torments or agonies of the body, so that there is nothing more grievous to ingenuous minds; for we see that many who are strong to bear want, courageous in torments, nay bold to meet death, do yet succumb under reproach. To obviate this evil Peter pronounces those blessed who are reproached for the sake of the Gospel, which is very contrary to what men commonly think and feel. Some read the words about the Spirit separately, as though it were, that which belongs to glory, and the Spirit of God; but the former reading, Calvin says, is more suitable as to the sense and simpler as to language. Peter shows that it is no hindrance to the happiness of the godly that they sustain reproach for the name of Christ, because they nevertheless retain a complete glory in the sight of God while the Spirit, who has glory ever connected with him, dwells in them; and it is enough for the godly that the Spirit of God testifies that the reproaches endured for the sake of the Gospel are blessed and full of glory. The Spirit of God was reproached, Calvin adds, because the unbelieving expose to ridicule whatever he suggests and dictates for our consolation; but the apostle would not have the eyes of the godly dazzled by this false opinion, and sets the hidden perception of faith, which God's children possess in their own hearts, in opposition to the presumption and insolence of the world. On the next verse Calvin says the apostle anticipates an objection, adding the reason why he had spoken only of that kind of trouble, even because they ought to have abstained from all evil-doing, lest they should do anything for which they might seem to be justly punished. Were any one to object that no one can be found so innocent but that he deserves for many faults to be chastised by God, Calvin replies that Peter here speaks of sins from which we ought to be entirely freed, such as thefts and murders, and further that the Apostle commands Christians to be such as they ought to be, pointing out a difference between us and the children of this world, who being without God's Spirit abandon themselves to every kind of wickedness. Though there are always many sins in the elect which God might justly punish, he adds, yet according to his paternal indulgence he spares his own children and does not inflict the punishment they deserve, and in the meantime, for honour's sake, adorns them with his own tokens and those of his Christ when he suffers them to be afflicted for the testimony of the Gospel. The unusual word seems to Calvin to designate one who covets what belongs to another, for they who gape after plunder or fraud inquire into the affairs of others with tortuous or crooked eyes. On the last verse Calvin says that, having forbidden the Christians to do any hurt, the apostle now bids them give thanks to God if they suffered persecution for the name of Christ; and truly it is no common kindness from God that he calls us, freed and exempted from the common punishment of our sins, to so honourable a warfare as to undergo for the testimony of his Gospel exiles, or prisons, or reproaches, or even death itself. Those are ungrateful to God who clamour or murmur on account of persecutions, as though they were unworthily dealt with, since on the contrary they ought to regard it as gain. When he says as a Christian, Calvin notes, he regards not so much the name as the cause: whatever reproachful words the adversaries made use of, it was enough for the faithful that they suffered for nothing else but for the defence of the Gospel.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson take the Spirit, the crimes and the name. Barnes says the sense of happy here is the same as blessed in the Beatitudes: they were to regard their condition as a blessed one, not that they would find personal enjoyment in being reproached, but because it would be like their Saviour's, would show that they were his friends, would be accompanied with rich spiritual influences here and followed by the rewards of heaven. There is no doubt, he says, that the Spirit of glory and of God is the Holy Spirit, and the meaning is that they might expect that Spirit to rest upon them if they were persecuted for the cause of Christ; there may be some allusion to the fact that the Spirit descended and abode on the Saviour at his baptism. The essential idea is that if they were called to suffer in the cause of the Redeemer they would not be left or forsaken, and they might hope that God would impart his Spirit in proportion to their sufferings; their persecutions are made the reason of a much more copious effusion of the Spirit on their souls, and hence it is often gain to the believer to suffer. On the next verse Barnes says that if they must suffer, they were to see that it was not for crime, and that even if such charges were brought no pretext should be furnished by their lives. The word rendered busybody occurs nowhere else in the New Testament and means properly an inspector of strange things, or of the things of others; a lexicographer supposes that it may refer to a director of heathenism, but the more obvious signification, and the one commonly adopted, is one who busies himself with what does not concern him, who pries into the affairs of another and attempts to control them as if they were his own. On the third verse Barnes says a man is not to be ashamed of religion so as to refuse to suffer on account of it, nor ashamed that he is despised and maltreated: he is not to be ashamed to be called a Christian, nor of the doctrines of his religion, nor of the Saviour, nor of the fellowship of true Christians however poor and despised, nor to have his name cast out. A man should be ashamed only of what is wrong, and should glory in what is right whatever the consequences to himself. Ellicott says the Spirit is called the Spirit of glory in the same way as he is called the Spirit of truth, of holiness and of grace, the word expressing that glory, the triumphant manifestation of perfections, is his gift and his distinguishing sign and the atmosphere in which he lives; glory stands in contrast with reproach, and lest it should be doubted who was meant by the splendid phrase the Apostle adds, and of God, so that the words form a climax, since God himself is greater than his own glory. The verb resteth means far more than remaineth or abideth: it expresses the complete repose and satisfaction with which the Spirit of glory abides on men who have the hearts of martyrs, and it is the word used of the quiet retreat our Lord took after John's death, of the calm relief he offers to the weary, and of the repose of the blessed dead; in the Old Testament it is used of the Spirit in Numbers and in 2 Kings, but above all in Isaiah 11:2, which was probably in Peter's mind. The argument, Ellicott says, is that reproach for the name of the Christ is a proof of glory in reserve, or rather already belonging to the man. On the next verse he notes that the Greek takes exactly the opposite turn, for let none of you suffer, and explains the connection: the apostle says advisedly that they are happy and that the Spirit reposes on those who die for the faith, because he is sure they will not try to deceive themselves and others by pretending to die as martyrs when in reality they are dying as criminals. To understand this caution, Ellicott says, we must recollect how largely the first converts were drawn from actually criminal classes and how easily they were admitted; in the persecution of Diocletian, Mensurius of Carthage found it necessary to expose those who drew persecution upon themselves to cloke their crimes under pretence of Christian faith, saying that some are criminals and some debtors who take the opportunity of persecution to be rid of so burdensome a life, thinking to atone for and wash off their misdeeds thereby. The insertion of as in the two latter cases obliterates the distinction between the class composed of those three words and that which follows, and it should read, as a murderer, or thief, or evildoer; when Pliny came to govern these men a little later he found that on a fixed day they met together before daylight and bound themselves by a sacramental oath, not to any crime, but that they would not do or see done any thefts, any robberies, any adulteries, that they would break no promises and would repudiate no liabilities when called upon. Of the last term Ellicott reports the observation that others, through excess of zeal, declaimed aloud against the pagans and cast their vices in their teeth, and their more sensible brethren humorously called them bishops or overseers of those who are without; such, he says, is indeed the meaning of the droll word Peter here gives, except that instead of bishops of those without it means bishops of other men's matters, denoting those prying and self-important people who fancy they can set everything to rights. On the third verse Ellicott says Peter purposely uses the name which was a name of derision among the heathens, not as yet one by which believers would usually describe themselves; it occurs only twice besides in the New Testament, where we are told of the invention of the nickname and where Agrippa catches it up with insolent scorn. So contemptible was the name that well-bred people avoided pronouncing it, or when forced to do so made a kind of apology, Tacitus saying, those who were vulgarly known by the name of Christians. It is quite an open question, Ellicott holds, whether we ought not here to read the nickname in its barbarous form, Chrestian: the Sinaitic manuscript has that form and the Vatican has Chreistian, and it is much harder to suppose that a scribe who commonly called himself a Christian would intentionally alter it into this strange form than to suppose that one who did not understand the irony should have written the word with which he was familiar. Let him not be ashamed, although the name sounds worse to the world than murderer or thief or malefactor; and the last clause is more pointedly rendered, but let him glorify God in this name, that is, make even this name of ridicule the ground of an act of glory to God. Robertson takes the condition as one of the first class assumed as true, notes that this is the only New Testament example of the bare phrase the name of Christ, used here because of the word Christian in the following verse, and observes the repetition of the article in the Greek though the word for Spirit occurs only once, the reference being to the Holy Spirit who is the Spirit of glory and of God. Resteth upon you is a quotation from Isaiah, and he quotes the comment that the Spirit rests upon the Christian as the Shechinah rested upon the tabernacle. On the next verse he notes the prohibition of a habit, two specific crimes and one general phrase and one unusual term, which was apparently coined by Peter from the words for belonging to another and overseer, the idea being one who spies out the affairs of other men; he collects several guesses, that it refers to things forbidden, to breaking up family relationships, to gadders-about and gossipers, and observes that the second element is the word for bishop and so suggests also preachers meddling in the work of other preachers. On the third verse he says the word Christian occurs only three times in the New Testament and is of Latin formation, coined to distinguish followers of Christ from Jews and Gentiles; it was not the usual term at first, the Jews using Nazarenes as a nickname, and by the sixties the name Christian was in common use in Rome, while owing to itacism it was sometimes spelled Chrestian. Peter had once been ashamed to suffer reproach or even a sneer for being a disciple of Christ, Robertson remarks, but Peter is not ashamed now.

Clarke and Wesley take the reproach, the variant reading and the honour. Clarke says that to be reproached for the name of Christ is to be reproached for being a Christian, that is, for being like Christ, which is the highest honour to which any man can arrive in this world. As the Divine Spirit rested upon Jesus, so does it rest upon his persecuted followers; and Clarke reports a various reading here, and of power, found in some of the chief manuscripts, in the later Syriac, in all the Arabic, Coptic, Ethiopic, Armenian and Vulgate, in some copies of the Itala, and in several fathers, so that the whole verse would read, if ye be reproached for the name of Christ, happy are ye, for the Spirit of glory, and of power, and of God, resteth upon you. This, he says, is agreeable to our Lord's words in the Beatitudes, so that what constituted them unhappy in the sight of the world was their chief happiness in the sight of God; they carried Christ, the fountain of blessedness, in their heart, and therefore could not be unhappy. The closing clause he renders, by them he is blasphemed, by you he is honoured. On the next verse Clarke glosses the unusual word as the inspector of another, meddling with other people's concerns and forgetting their own, such persons being hated of all men; but some think, he adds, that meddling with those in public office is here intended, as if the apostle had said, meddle not with the affairs of state, leave public offices and public officers to their own master, strive to live peaceably with all men, and show yourselves humble and unaspiring. On the last verse Clarke says that if a man be persecuted because he has embraced the Christian faith, let him not be ashamed but rather glorify God on this very account: Christ suffered by the Jews because he was holy, and Christians suffer because they resemble him. Wesley says reproaches and cruel mockings were always one part of their sufferings, and that the same Spirit which was upon Christ is here termed the Spirit of glory, conquering all reproach and shame, and the Spirit of God, whose Son Jesus Christ is; while they are blaspheming Christ, the readers glorify him in the midst of their sufferings. On the next verse Wesley says none is to suffer deservedly, as an evildoer, in any kind; and on the last, that the sufferer is to glorify God, who gives him the honour so to suffer and so great a reward for suffering.

debates: Whether the words and of power belong to the text. Clarke reports the reading as found in some of the chief manuscripts and in the later Syriac, the Arabic, Coptic, Ethiopic, Armenian and Vulgate versions and several fathers, and gives the whole verse with it; Calvin notices instead a different division of the received words, that which belongs to glory and the Spirit of God, but prefers the ordinary reading as simpler and more suitable; the others translate without a variant.

What the fourth crime is. Barnes takes it as one who busies himself with what does not concern him, and reports the guess that it means a director of heathenism; Clarke gives the same and adds a political reading, that meddling with those in public office may be meant; Ellicott calls it a droll word meaning bishops of other men's matters; Robertson thinks the apostle coined it, collects several guesses and notes that its second element is the word for bishop; Calvin dissents from all and makes it covetousness, the gaping after another's goods.

What weight the name Christian carries. Ellicott says it was then a name of derision that well-bred people avoided pronouncing, and holds it an open question whether the barbarous form Chrestian should not be read, since the oldest manuscripts have it; Robertson reports the same spelling and the same contempt and notes that the Jews used Nazarenes instead; Gill says the name was first given at Antioch and, being agreeable, was retained; Calvin regards not the name but the cause.
outliers: Ellicott alone explains the caution against crime from the state of the early Church, recalling that converts were largely drawn from criminal classes and citing a bishop who had to expose men that courted persecution to cloak their crimes and wash off their misdeeds.
Robertson alone turns the exhortation back on its author, remarking that the apostle had once been ashamed of a mere sneer for being a disciple of Christ, and that he is not ashamed now.

17.pericope_label: For the time is come that judgment must begin at the house of God: and if it first begin at us, what shall the end be of them that obey not the gospel of God? And if the righteous scarcely be saved, where shall the ungodly and the sinner appear?

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin define the house and the judgment. Gill says that by the house of God is either meant the temple at Jerusalem, which is often so called because it was built for God and where were the symbol of his presence and his worship, and now the time was come that God would begin at his sanctuary and leave this house desolate, not one stone being left upon another, as Christ had foretold; or else the church of God, which is frequently called the house of God because it is of his building, where he dwells and grants his gracious presence, and which he beautifies, fills, repairs and defends, so that it may design believers in Christ, those of the household and family of God. By judgment, Gill says, is meant not punishment for sin, strictly speaking, because Christ has endured this in the room and stead of his church and people and therefore in justice it cannot be inflicted on them, but afflictions and persecutions, which are fatherly chastisements, and different from God's judgment on the world and condemnation with it. On the next verse Gill says the righteous are such not as are so in their own opinion or merely in the esteem of others, nor on account of their morality and external righteousness before men or by the deeds of the law, but who are made righteous by the righteousness of Christ imputed to them; and such are scarcely saved, not as if they were but in part saved, for they are completely saved, Christ having wrought out and finished a complete salvation for them, and they are saved from all enemies and from everything that might hurt them, from sin, Satan, the law, the world, hell and death, and are completely justified and have all their sins pardoned. Nor is it as if their salvation were doubtful, Gill adds, for though they are scarcely, yet certainly saved, since they are chosen to salvation, and Christ has obtained it for them, and they have the application of it already made to them by the blessed Spirit. Calvin says the apostle amplifies the consolation which the goodness of the cause for which we suffer brings to us, for this necessity awaits the whole Church of God, not only to be subject to the common miseries of men but especially to be chastised by the hand of God; with more submission, then, ought persecutions for Christ to be endured, for unless we desire to be blotted out from the number of the faithful we must submit our backs to the scourges of God. It is a sweet consolation, Calvin says, that God does not execute his judgments on us as on others, but that he makes us the representatives of his own Son, when we do not suffer except for his cause and for his name. Peter took this sentence, he thinks, from the common and constant teaching of Scripture, and this seems more probable to him than that a certain passage is referred to; it was formerly usual with the Lord, as all the prophets witness, to exhibit the first examples of his chastisements in his own people, as the head of a family corrects his own children rather than those of strangers. Though God is the judge of the whole world, he would have his providence to be especially acknowledged in the government of his own Church. On the next verse Calvin says that when the faithful see that it is well with the wicked they are necessarily tempted to be envious, and this is a very dangerous trial, since present happiness is what all desire; the Spirit of God therefore dwells on this carefully in many places, lest the faithful should envy the prosperity of the ungodly. Peter shows that afflictions ought to be calmly borne by the children of God when they compare the lot of others with their own, taking it as granted that God is the judge of the world and that therefore no one can escape his hand with impunity, and inferring that a dreadful vengeance will soon overtake those whose condition seems now favourable. The argument, Calvin says, is from the less to the greater: if God spares not his own children whom he loves and who obey him, how dreadful will be his severity against enemies and such as are rebellious; there is nothing better, then, than to obey the Gospel, so that God may kindly correct us by his paternal hand for our salvation. It has been thought, he adds, that this sentence is taken from Proverbs, for the Greek translators have thus rendered what Solomon says.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson identify the house and weigh the quotation. Barnes says the time is come means that this trial is now to be expected, and probably the apostle referred to some indications then apparent. The word rendered judgment seems to mean the severe trial which would determine character, referring to such calamities as would settle the question whether there was any religion, or would test the value of that which was professed; it was to begin at the house of God, or be applied to the church first, in order that the nature and worth of religion might be seen. Benson, Bloomfield and many others suppose the phrase refers to the Jews and to the calamities about to come around the temple and the holy city, but the more obvious reference, Barnes says, is to Christians, spoken of as the house or family of God, and there is probably an allusion to the vision in Ezekiel where the destroyer is told to slay utterly and to begin at the sanctuary. On the next verse Barnes traces the word rendered scarcely through its other occurrences and says it implies that there is some difficulty or obstruction, so that the thing came very near not to happen, or so that there was much risk about it. The apostle seems to have had his eye on a verse in Proverbs and has merely expanded and illustrated it; by the question he employs he admits that the righteous are saved with difficulty, or that there are perils which jeopard their salvation and which are of such a kind as to make it very near not to happen. They would indeed be saved, Barnes says, but it would be in such a manner as to show that the circumstances were such as to render it, to human appearances, doubtful and problematical, and this peril may have arisen from many circumstances, the first being the difficulty of forming a plan of salvation, involving a degree of wisdom wholly beyond that of man. Ellicott says the word for seems to substantiate the whole of the former part of the section, with special reference to the injunction to glorify God on the ground of bearing the name of Christians: the judgment is just about to begin, and all those who bear the name may well be thankful that they do. It should be, that the judgment, that is the great judgment which we all expect; but the word begin shows that in Peter's mind it would be a long process, and he probably does not distinguish between the burning which is befalling for a trial and the final judgment, except that the burning is but the beginning. The phrase about the house of God contains an obvious reference to Ezekiel, and who are meant is clear not only from other passages but from the immediate addition, and if first at us: we who bear the mark of the Christ's shame upon our foreheads, and are not ashamed of it, are quite safe in this judgment, since the word was, come not near any man upon whom is the mark. On the next verse Ellicott says this is a literal quotation, word for word, of Proverbs 11:31 according to the Greek version, and that the quotation proves Peter's perfect familiarity with both the Hebrew original and the Greek version, since we have seen how he rejects that version when it does not suit his meaning, while here it suits him, though it differs from the Hebrew, and he accepts it. The righteous man here means, as Leighton says, he that endeavours to walk uprightly in the ways of God, rather than the man who is then declared finally justified; and the fact that they are scarcely saved imports not, according to Leighton, any uncertainty or hazard in the thing itself to the end, in respect of the purpose and performance of God, but only the great difficulties and hard encounters in the way. This, Ellicott says, is only partly true: the Apostle is rather thinking of the final judgment than of the life of trial, and he means that there was but little margin left, a very few more falls, a few more refusals to follow the calls of grace, and they would have been lost; doubtless, when the best of us looks back, in the light of the last day, upon all that he has been through, he will be amazed that he ever could be saved at all. The ungodly and the sinner is the Gentile character, ungodly denoting open irreligion, contempt of God and all that belongs to his worship, while sinner goes more to the moral side of the nature, pointing most of all to sins of the flesh. Robertson notes that there is no predicate in the first phrase and that what follows comes from the vision of Ezekiel; the construction is unusual, not exactly purpose or result and almost in apposition. The persecution on hand was a foretaste of more to come, and by house of God he can mean the same as the spiritual house of the second chapter, or a local church, while one commentator even takes it to refer to the family. On the next verse Robertson notes the first-class condition and the quotation from Proverbs, and enters one caution, that the Christian is not saved by his own righteousness.

Clarke and Wesley read the judgment historically and compare the versions. Clarke says our Lord had predicted that previously to the destruction of Jerusalem his own followers would have to endure various calamities, and that here his true disciples are called the house or family of God; that the converted Jews suffered much from their own brethren, the zealots or factions into which the Jews were then divided, needs little proof, and some interpreters think this was in conformity to the purpose of God, that the Jewish Christians were to be involved in the general punishment, and that it was proper to begin at them as a part of the devoted Jewish nation, notwithstanding they were now become the house of God, because the justice of God would thereby be more illustriously displayed. But probably the word which we here translate judgment, Clarke says, may mean no more than affliction and distress, for it was a Jewish maxim that when God was about to pour down some general judgment he began with afflicting his own people in order to correct and amend them, that they might be prepared for the overflowing scourge; and in a rabbinic treatise we have the same sentiment, and in nearly the same words as in Peter, that God never punishes the world but because of the wicked, yet he always begins with the righteous first, the destroyer making no difference between the just and the unjust, only he begins first with the righteous. On the next verse Clarke asks, if it shall be with extreme difficulty that the Christians shall escape from Jerusalem when the Roman armies come against it with full commission to destroy it, where shall the ungodly and the sinner appear, where shall the proud boaster in his own outside holiness and the profligate transgressor show themselves as having escaped the divine vengeance? The Christians, though with difficulty, did escape, every man, but not one of the Jews escaped, whether found in Jerusalem or elsewhere. It is rather strange, Clarke says, but it is a fact, that this verse is the Greek version of Proverbs 11:31, where the Hebrew runs, behold, to the righteous it shall be returned on the earth, and also to the wicked and the transgressor; such a latitude of construction can scarcely be accounted for. He then sets out the Chaldee paraphrast, which says the righteous shall be strengthened in the earth but the ungodly and the sinners shall be consumed from it; the Syriac, which says if the righteous scarcely live, where shall the ungodly and the sinner stand; the Arabic, which is nearly the same as the Greek and the apostle; and the Latin, which follows the Hebrew. Clarke adds that when Cestius Gallus came against Jerusalem many Christians were shut up in it, and when he strangely raised the siege the Christians immediately departed to Pella. Wesley says the time is come for judgment to begin at the house of God, since God first visits his church, and that both in justice and mercy; and how terribly will he visit those who obey not the gospel, since the judgments which are milder at the beginning grow more and more severe, while good men, having already sustained their part, are only spectators of the miseries of the wicked. On the next verse Wesley glosses scarcely saved as escaping with the utmost difficulty, and the ungodly as the man who knows not God, and adds that the salvation here primarily spoken of is of a temporal nature, but that we may apply the words to eternal things, and then they are still more awful.

debates: What the house of God is. Gill allows either the temple at Jerusalem, about to be left desolate, or the church; Barnes reports that many refer it to the Jews and the doom of the holy city but holds the obvious reference to be Christians, and finds an allusion to the vision in Ezekiel; Ellicott takes it the same way and presses the following words, and if first at us; Robertson allows the spiritual house of the second chapter, a local church, or even the family; Clarke calls the true disciples the house or family of God and supplies a rabbinic maxim to the same effect.

Whether a particular text is quoted at the first verse. Barnes and Ellicott both find an allusion to Ezekiel, where the destroyer is told to begin at the sanctuary, and Robertson says the phrase comes from that vision; Calvin denies that any particular passage is meant, holding that the apostle took the sentence from the common and constant teaching of Scripture, since God always exhibited the first examples of his chastisements in his own people.

In what sense the righteous are scarcely saved. Barnes grants that there are perils which jeopard their salvation, so that to human appearance it was doubtful; Gill denies both that they are but in part saved and that their salvation is doubtful, holding that though scarcely, yet certainly they are saved; Ellicott reports the opinion that scarcely imports no uncertainty in the thing itself but only difficulty in the way, and answers that this is only partly true, since the apostle thinks of the final judgment and means that little margin was left; Robertson adds that the Christian is not saved by his own righteousness.

What to make of the quotation differing from the Hebrew. Ellicott calls it a literal quotation of the Greek version and evidence of the apostle's familiarity with both texts, since he rejects that version elsewhere when it does not suit him and accepts it here; Clarke calls the same fact rather strange and says such a latitude of construction can scarcely be accounted for, setting the Hebrew, Chaldee, Syriac, Arabic and Latin side by side.
outliers: Ellicott alone joins the two halves of the chapter, taking the mark of Ezekiel's vision for the very name of Christian borne without shame, so that those who wear it are the men the destroyer is forbidden to touch.

Wesley alone reads the salvation on two levels, holding that the escape primarily spoken of is of a temporal kind while the words may be applied to eternal things, in which case they are still more awful.

19.pericope_label: Wherefore let them that suffer according to the will of God commit the keeping of their souls to him in well doing, as unto a faithful Creator.

schools.summary: Gill and Calvin draw the conclusion and weigh the last title. Gill says this is the conclusion made from the foregoing premises: seeing that the state and condition of the saints in this world, at worst, and which is but for a time, is infinitely preferable to the dreadful state of disobedient persons, ungodly men and sinners, which will endure to all eternity, they should not think strange of their sufferings or complain of them but patiently endure them. Especially, Gill says, when they consider that these are not the effects of chance, nor merely owing to the malice and wickedness of men, or to any second cause only, but they are the will of God, are by his appointment, under his direction and by his order, and are for their good and his own glory. Calvin draws the conclusion that persecutions ought to be submissively endured, for the condition of the godly in them is much happier than that of the unbelieving, who enjoy prosperity to their utmost wishes. He reminds us, however, that we suffer nothing except according to the permission of God, which tends much to comfort us; and the exhortation is the same as though the apostle had said, let them deliver themselves and their life to the safe keeping of God. He calls him faithful, Calvin says, because he faithfully keeps and defends whatever is under his protection or power. Some render the word Creator, and the Greek term means both, but Calvin prefers the former meaning, that of a keeper, for by bidding us to deposit our life with God the apostle makes him its safe keeper. The words in well-doing are added, he notes, lest the faithful should retaliate the wrongs done to them, but that they might on the contrary contend with the ungodly who injured them by well-doing.

Barnes, Ellicott and Robertson define the deposit and the title. Barnes says those who suffer according to the will of God are those who endure the kind of sufferings that he, by his Providence, shall appoint; and since there is so much danger, since there is no one else who can keep them, and since he is a Being so faithful, let them commit all their interests to him. The word rendered souls is equivalent to themselves: they were to leave everything in his hand, faithfully performing every duty and not being anxious for the result. In well doing means constantly doing good, or seeking to perform every duty in a proper manner, their business being always to do right and the result to be left with God; a man who is engaged always in well-doing, Barnes says, may safely commit all his interest to God. God may be trusted, or confided in, in all his attributes and in all the relations which he sustains as Creator, Redeemer, Moral Governor and Judge, and in all these we may come before him with confidence and put unwavering trust in him. As Creator particularly, as one who has brought us and all creatures and things into being, we may be sure that he will be faithful to the design which he had in view; from that design he will never depart until it is fully accomplished, since he abandons no purpose which he has formed, and we may be assured that he will faithfully pursue it to the end. As our Creator we may come to him and look to him for his protection and care: he made us, he had a design in our creation, and he so endowed us that we might live for ever and honour and enjoy him; he did not create us that we might be miserable, nor does he wish it, but formed us in such a way that, if we choose, we may be eternally happy, and in the path he has appointed us to go we may be sure of his aid and protection. Ellicott says the word wherefore looks back to the fact that the beginning of the judgment, the judgment of the Christians, is so light in comparison with the fearful end when it lights on the disobedient and wicked. Our version, he notes, omits an important little word: it should be, let them that suffer also, or, let even them that suffer, according to the will of God, the stress being on the suffering, that is, on being put to death. The clause about the will of God seems not intended to mean in a godly and unblameable manner, as opposed to the suffering as a murderer of the fifteenth verse; rather it brings out that such a death is no accident, no sudden calamity, but in strict accordance with God's prearranged design, and thus it harmonises with what follows about a faithful Creator and the committing of souls. The beautiful verb rendered commit the keeping of, Ellicott says, is a technical term for depositing a deed, or sum of money, or other valuable, with any one in trust; in the literal sense it occurs in Luke and in 2 Timothy, in a metaphorical sense of doctrines committed in trust to the safe keeping of the Episcopate, and of leaving persons whom you love in trust in the Acts. But the words which Peter probably has ringing in his ears when he thus writes are the words of our Lord on the cross, where the same verb is used, Father, into Thy hands I commend My spirit. Their souls might perhaps, with still more propriety, be here translated their lives, and the connection will then be: consider the mildness of these trials compared with the terrors overhanging the sinful; even if the worst should come to the worst and you must die a martyr's death, it is but the execution of God's plan for you; view your life as a deposit, lay it confidently in His hands, to be returned to you again when the time comes, and you will find Him faithful to what a Creator ought to be. The word faithful, Ellicott adds, is used in reference to the deposit placed in His hands, and the title Creator seems to be chosen here rather than Father. Robertson says the opening word picks up the thread of consolation again, and parses the present continuous middle imperative of an old word, a banking figure, to deposit, the word used by Jesus as he died. The phrase in well-doing is a late and rare word occurring only here in the New Testament.

Clarke and Wesley take the suffering morally and attach a condition. Clarke says a man suffers according to the will of God who suffers for righteousness' sake, and who, being reviled, reviles not again; and to commit the keeping of their souls is to place their lives confidently in his hand, who, being their Creator, will also be their preserver, and keep that safely which is committed to his trust. God is here represented as faithful, Clarke says, because he will always fulfil his promises and withhold no good thing from them that walk uprightly; but they had no reason to hope that he would care for their lives and souls unless they continued in well-doing, since he who is employed in God's work will have God's protection, and the path of duty ever was, and ever will be, the only way of safety. Clarke closes the chapter with two observations: that the apostle recommends fervent charity, unfeigned love both to God and man, a universal virtue which ought to precede, accompany and follow all others, since a charity which has God for its principle and Jesus Christ for its pattern never faileth, and if our charity be extensive enough to cover all the defects of our neighbour in bearing with them, that of God is sufficient to cover all the sins of a sincere penitent by blotting them out; and that the difficulty of escaping the corruption that is in the world is great, and consequently the danger of losing our souls, so that in this great work watchfulness, prayer, faith and obedience are indispensably necessary, and he who does not walk with God here cannot see nor enjoy him hereafter. Wesley says those suffer according to the will of God who suffer both for a good cause and in a right spirit, and that they are to commit to him their souls, whatever becomes of the body, as a sacred depositum; in well doing, this being their care, to do and suffer well, while he will take care of the rest, as unto a faithful Creator, in whose truth, love and power they may safely trust.

debates: What suffering according to the will of God means. Clarke takes it morally, of one who suffers for righteousness' sake and, being reviled, reviles not again, and Wesley of suffering both for a good cause and in a right spirit; Ellicott refuses that reading and holds the clause to mean that such a death is no accident but stands in strict accordance with God's prearranged design; Barnes and Gill go the same way, Gill insisting that the sufferings are not the effects of chance nor merely of men's malice.

Whether the word should be souls or lives. Ellicott says it might with still more propriety be rendered lives, and builds his paraphrase on the deposit being returned when the time comes; Barnes takes it as equivalent to themselves, so that everything is left in God's hand; Wesley adds the qualification, whatever becomes of the body.

What the last title means. Calvin says the Greek word means both creator and keeper and prefers the second, since by bidding us deposit our life with God the apostle makes him its safe keeper; Ellicott keeps Creator and remarks that the title seems chosen here rather than Father; Barnes builds on the title at length, that God will be faithful to the design he had in our creation and abandons no purpose he has formed; Clarke joins Creator and preserver in one.

How far the promise is conditional. Clarke attaches a condition, that they had no reason to hope God would care for their lives and souls unless they continued in well-doing, the path of duty being the only way of safety; Barnes states the same balance more mildly, that a man engaged always in well-doing may safely commit all his interest to God; Calvin turns the phrase against retaliation, that they should contend with those who injured them by well-doing.
outliers: Ellicott alone notes an omitted particle in the English, holding that it should read, let even them that suffer, so that the stress falls on being put to death rather than on the manner of the suffering.
Calvin alone declines the rendering Creator, preferring keeper on the ground that the apostle, having bidden us deposit our life with God, is naming him the safe keeper of the deposit.
themes: suffer according to the will of God
commit the keeping of their souls
